articles.title: ‘Don’t wait for somebody else to fix it’: T-Mobile exec Deeanne King on cutting CO2 and costs
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: When Deeanne King came to the Pacific Northwest in 2020 — relocating from Kansas after Sprint merged with Bellevue, Wash.-based T-Mobile — she fell in love with the region’s natural beauty. In her role as executive vice president and chief people officer, she also helps lead sustainability efforts for the telecom giant.
“The outdoors is my happy place,” King said. The region’s lakes, inland sea and trails, she added, are “a good reminder of what we’re all working to protect.”

T-Mobile has been ranked among the greenest companies in the U.S and globally. It’s making notable progress toward climate goals at a time when numerous corporations are scaling back or abandoning their carbon targets.
Keep reading to learn more about King’s sustainability journey. Her quotes have been edited for clarity and length.
What gives you the most hope for the planet?

People. Hands down. I get to work with some incredibly smart, curious, and committed people, and one thing I’ve learned is that when you put a hard problem in front of people who care, they find a way. They challenge the status quo, they try something new, they learn, and they keep going. I’ve never seen our teams walk away from a problem because it was hard.

I’m also encouraged by the growing recognition that sustainability and good business can, and should, go together. Building more efficiently, using resources more thoughtfully, and reducing waste can make a business more resilient while also being better for the planet. Those things don’t have to compete.

And I see that mindset in our employees. People want their work to matter. They want to contribute to something bigger than themselves. When you combine that sense of purpose with ingenuity and a willingness to work together, I think there’s tremendous reason for hope.
What’s one habit you’ve changed personally because of environmental concerns?
I’ve gotten much more intentional about cutting down on single-use things, and my reusable water bottle is probably the simplest example. It goes everywhere with me now.

It sounds small, but I think that’s actually the point. Once you make one change part of your routine, you start noticing other opportunities: what you throw away, what you reuse, what you buy, and what you probably didn’t need in the first place. Those small choices add up.
Coffee with any sustainability leader, past or present — who do you pick?

I’d choose Chief Sustainability Officer Kara Hurst at Amazon. T-Mobile joined Amazon and hundreds of other companies in signing the Climate Pledge, committing to reach net-zero carbon by 2040. And there’s something Kara has said about that work that really resonates with me: “We cannot go at this alone.”

I couldn’t agree more. The biggest challenges we face aren’t going to be solved by one company, one industry, or one really smart person. We have to find common ground, share what we’re learning, and be willing to work together toward something bigger than any one of us.

I’d love to sit down with Kara and compare notes on what’s working, where we’re getting stuck, and where companies like ours can work together to move faster. And knowing me, we’d probably end up talking about people and leadership too, because ultimately, ambitious goals only become real when you have people who are willing to question how things have always been done and figure out how to get there.
What’s an underrated solution that deserves more attention?

Making sustainability practical. Sometimes we gravitate toward the giant, breakthrough idea, and we absolutely need those. But there is also enormous opportunity in doing the basics really, really well and using data to figure out where small changes can add up to a very big impact.

Take buildings. They aren’t necessarily the first thing people think about when they think about climate innovation, but managing HVAC systems more intelligently produced nearly $5 million in estimated energy savings for T-Mobile in 2025. As of 2025, we have 132 community solar projects in our portfolio, providing an estimated lifetime total savings of $60 million in energy costs. You can reduce energy use, lower costs, and do something positive for the planet.
What’s one metric you watch obsessively as a sustainability leader?

I don’t know that I would use the word obsessively, but I absolutely believe in measuring whether the work is actually making a difference. One number I’m particularly proud of is that in 2025, T-Mobile’s total emissions were 50% lower than our 2020 baseline. That’s meaningful progress, especially because our business hasn’t been standing still.
The scope of the climate challenge is daunting — how do you approach this work?

You can’t let the size of the problem become the reason you don’t start. That’s true of climate change, but honestly, it’s true of almost every really hard problem I’ve encountered in my career. When something feels enormous, I focus first on what we can control. What’s the next decision? What’s the next action? What can we make better today? Then you keep going.
I’m also a big believer in being willing to learn along the way. Take smart risks, look at the data, listen to people, adjust and keep moving.
What impact do you hope your work has in 20 years?

As a mom, I think about the world we’re handing to the next generation. Of course I want my children, and someday, their children, to inherit a healthy planet. But I also want them to inherit the belief that when something matters, you don’t wait for somebody else to fix it. You figure out what you can do, you bring people together and you get to work.

articles.title: Amazon challenges Nvidia’s software advantage with new tool for its own AI chips
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: A new software tool from Amazon aims to make switching from Nvidia to the company’s own AI chips about as simple as changing a setting.

The software, dubbed TorchNeuron, runs code written in PyTorch, the open-source framework used by many AI developers, on Amazon’s Trainium chips. It has been in private beta since late last year, and Amazon said Monday that it’s opening the software to all developers as a public beta .

Until now, developers who wanted to run PyTorch code on Trainium had to modify it to call programming interfaces specific to Amazon’s chips, said Colin Brace , vice president of technology software at Annapurna Labs, Amazon’s chip-design unit. With TorchNeuron, the same code runs after a basic configuration change.
“If you know PyTorch, then you know Trainium,” Brace said in an interview.

Nvidia dominates the market for AI chips, partly because much of the industry’s AI software was built around its CUDA platform. Adapting that code to other hardware can take months of engineering work. That has made many companies reluctant to switch, even as Amazon, Google and others have developed their own chips.
TorchNeuron is part of a broader push by tech giants to loosen Nvidia’s grip on AI computing, even as they remain among its biggest customers.

Asked about Amazon’s relationship with Nvidia, Brace said the company has “always been about choice,” pointing to another high-profile example: AWS offers Intel processors alongside its own Graviton chips.
Amazon plans to release TorchNeuron as open-source software on Tuesday in conjunction with the PyTorch Conference in San Jose, Calif.

Trainium’s biggest users so far are AI labs with close financial ties to Amazon. Anthropic, in which Amazon has invested billions , uses the chips to train and run its Claude models. OpenAI agreed in February to use 2 gigawatts of Trainium capacity as part of a deal in which Amazon is investing $50 billion in the company.
Brace said Amazon’s goal has always been wide use of the chips, calling TorchNeuron “an accelerant” along those lines.

Amazon’s chip business traces back to its 2015 acquisition of Annapurna Labs , an Israeli chipmaker, for a reported $350 million. The Annapurna team went on to design Trainium as well as Amazon’s Graviton processors.

In his annual shareholder letter in April, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy wrote that the company’s chip business, including Trainium and Graviton, had an annual revenue run rate of more than $20 billion. He estimated that figure would be about $50 billion if the chips were sold to AWS and other customers by a standalone chip business.
“There’s so much demand for our chips that it’s quite possible we’ll sell racks of them to third parties in the future,” he wrote.

More than 30 companies and internal Amazon teams have been using TorchNeuron during the private beta. Deepgram, a San Francisco startup that makes speech AI, says its benchmarks showed Trainium processing about 60% more audio per dollar than its existing GPU setup. The company now runs Trainium in production, Brace said.

Inside Amazon, the Prime Video team used TorchNeuron to build Prime 360 , an AI system that reconstructs NBA plays in 3D so viewers can watch replays from angles a traditional camera can’t capture. The feature, which runs on Trainium, will appear on select Prime Video broadcasts this NBA season.

To make sure TorchNeuron works with the huge variety of AI models that developers build, Amazon tests it every night against more than 100,000 models from Hugging Face, the popular online hub for open-source AI, Brace said.
Brace said the timing of the project reflects changes in PyTorch itself. The framework has matured, and its maintainers have been working to make it less dependent on any one kind of hardware.

Amazon has contributed to that effort, removing code that tied PyTorch to specific chips. Newer versions of PyTorch can detect which hardware they’re running on, he said, so in some cases developers don’t need to change their code at all.

articles.title: Microsoft unveils tools to monitor and corral rogue AI agents
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Microsoft is coming out with new security tools that treat AI agents as potential insider threats, continuously assessing their risk and restricting their access when something changes.
The features, announced Monday, are part of Microsoft 365 E7, the company’s top-tier bundle of workplace software and AI tools, and its Project Perception security system.
They escalate the company’s competition with rivals such as Google, Amazon Web Services, CrowdStrike and Okta to become the system businesses use to control their AI agents.

Microsoft’s new features come amid a steady stream of news about AI agents doing things they weren’t supposed to do, including high-profile reports from Anthropic about test agents taking unauthorized actions on government websites, and from OpenAI about agents escaping test environments and stealing credentials.
The move builds on Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella’s Oct. 10 blog post arguing that the controls on AI models need to come from outside the models themselves.
“The most trustworthy Super Intelligence system will not be the one with the model we trust most,” Nadella wrote. “It will be the one that enables us to trust the model the least.”

Microsoft’s tools include a continuously updated risk assessment for each agent, based on signals such as what data it can reach and whether its actions are starting to depart from the task it was given. When the risk level rises, the system can take away the agent’s ability to make changes while still letting it read data, require a person to approve a high-stakes step, or shut the agent down.

In addition, the company is expanding its ability to find AI agents running on employees’ computers, increasing the number of agent types it can detect to 60, up from 25. The list includes popular tools such as Anthropic’s Claude Code, OpenAI’s Codex and GitHub Copilot.

Microsoft is also adding “Guardian Agents” to Project Perception, an AI security system it unveiled in July that uses AI agents to find and fix security problems. The new agents can investigate why another agent’s risk changed and recommend or take steps to contain it.
The company’s new features are in private preview, with broader availability planned for Microsoft’s Ignite conference, Nov. 17-19 in San Francisco.

The E7 licensing level , which launched in May, costs $99 per user per month. It also includes the Microsoft 365 Copilot AI assistant, the company’s E5 suite of productivity and security tools, its Entra Suite identity tools and Agent 365, a service for managing AI agents.

articles.title: Housing Accountability Act Puts Tiny Beaux Arts Village in the Spotlight
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Changes to state law intended to broaden access to more affordable types of housing are reverberating in some unexpected places, including within Puget Sound's smallest jurisdictions. Last week, the town council in Beaux Arts Village – population 310 – met to approve a slate of temporary zoning changes, under threat of state sanctions and prompted by the 2025 Housing Accountability Act. While the vote was unanimous, the meeting included plenty of hand-wringing about the path the town had taken to get to that point.

Clocking in at just 0.17 square miles, Beaux Arts Village is a town entirely ensconced within the City of Bellevue, a pocket of narrow, tree-lined streets where golf carts are more commonplace than apartment buildings. Founded in 1908 as an artist's colony, the town's initial boosters drew residents with advertisements in the Seattle Times touting the fledgling community as "an expedition into the realms of Utopia." The town's primary amenity is a 1,100 foot stretch of beach, which only town property owners have access to as members of a separate, non-profit organization known as the Western Academy of Beaux Arts.

In 1954, Beaux Arts officially incorporated, to "protect the beach and the Village lifestyle," according to the town's website today. It had taken two years for Beaux Arts to reach the required 300-resident minimum necessary to be able to become a town, but just over seven decades later the population has only changed by six residents. Today, the median home value in Beaux Arts Village is $2.6 million.

In the decades since the implementation of Washington's 1990 Growth Management Act (GMA), the state-mandated growth plans in enclaves like Beaux Arts Village haven't traditionally been subjected to much scrutiny. But in 2025, the state legislature passed the Housing Accountability Act , empowering the Washington Department of Commerce to directly evaluate whether local jurisdictions are meeting the expectations laid out in state law when it comes to accommodating housing. Before that law was approved, the only avenue for a local Comprehensive Plan to be found inadequate was through a citizen appeal – though the state has sometimes taken the drastic step of making that appeal itself in extreme circumstances.

In January, Commerce announced that Beaux Arts Village had been selected as one of the first eight jurisdictions ever subjected to "selected review" under the Housing Accountability Act. As part of that review, agency staff have been tasked with determining whether all eight are in compliance with all aspects of the GMA, including new provisions that direct localities to plan for housing across different income levels – requirements that many cities have found vexing.

Beaux Arts' 2024 Comprehensive Plan was reviewed with a fine-toothed comb, and in June a preliminary report was issued to town officials that listed everything that needed to be adjusted to get into alignment with state law, in Commerce's view. That letter gave town officials their marching orders, and started the clock.

"We've been at it for nine months. We presented a Comp Plan that I think is in alignment with what everybody here will believe is keeping with what the village is, which has been much like the past three or four Comp Plans that we put together," Beaux Arts Councilmember Tom Stowe said Tuesday. "Commerce came in and shredded it, basically, and said that we couldn't do what we basically wanted."

Beaux Arts Village's share of Puget Sound's expected housing growth over the coming decades is not substantial. In fact, when King County handed out housing growth targets across all 39 cities and towns countywide in 2021 – an expectation of the number of new units to plan for through 2044 – the number was just one. Its neighbor Bellevue is planning for 35,000.

And yet the town's existing land use, intended to preserve a "tranquil, calm living environment" per the current Beaux Arts Village Comprehensive Plan, has presented certain challenges when it comes to growth plan compliance. Per a 2021 adjustment to the GMA known as House Bill 1220, Beaux Arts Village is required to plan for that one housing unit to be occupied by a household making 30% of King County's median area income or below – households that overall have the greatest difficulty finding housing.

30% of King County's median income is just under $40,000 for a family of two, and residents bringing in that little income cannot afford the single family homes that make up the vast majority of the town's housing stock, nor can they afford the backyard cottages that are allowed on those lots either.

To make it feasible to build at least one home that could be within reach to that future low-income household, Commerce recommended that Beaux Arts Village officials adjust zoning to allow some type of multifamily housing within their borders. Beaux Arts ultimately settled on the idea of creating a co-living "overlay." Co-living housing, also referred to as single-room occupancy (SRO) homes, provide the lowest rents even when built without any subsidy.

Though the idea of allowing six units of co-living housing just on one block of Beaux Arts Village was considered by the town planning commission, but counting on six property owners to build that specific type of housing would likely fall short of providing the necessary capacity. Instead, a proposal advanced that would allow co-living housing outside of the town's "erosion control hazard area" closest to Lake Washington.

The Beaux Arts Village planning commission deadlocked 2-2 on the idea of scaling back Commerce's recommendation to allow six co-living units on all lots in the overlay, but the town council ultimately did scale that number back to four. The fewer units allowed in the overlay, the less likely that it is that any actual co-living projects will get built – an outcome that did come up Tuesday.
"If we think this is about somebody coming in and building, nobody is going to build this," Councilmember Stacy Saal said.

As a town of its size, there is no Beaux Arts Village town hall – just a town mailbox. Town council meetings take place in a rotating councilmember's home, which is how a dining room and adjoining kitchen was transformed into a public meeting room last week for the monthly town council. Twenty to thirty Beaux Arts residents packed into the space, standing in the hallway or sitting on the floor as their elected representatives debated town matters, including whether to get in compliance with state housing law.

The big incentive for councilmembers to act and adopt the interim ordinance, which will expire February 4, was the stick included in the Housing Accountability Act. In addition to being disqualified for some state grants, cities and towns deemed to be out of compliance with the GMA trigger what is known as the Builder's Remedy .

A brand new provision in state law, the Builder's Remedy requires the approval of any complete building permit – no matter whether the underlying project conflicts with the underlying zoning for the site, as long as certain requirements for on-site affordable units are met. Theoretically, this could lead to a ten story apartment building in Beaux Arts Village, as long as a subset of the new units are kept within certain rents.

"If we don't do this tonight, as you all remember, the consequence is we go out of compliance, and the low income builder remedy kicks in, and any low income builder comes in and can submit plans that totally ignore our zoning code, they can come in and build whatever they want," Beaux Arts Mayor Aletha Howes the crowd in attendance on Tuesday. "The only thing they have to follow is setbacks and tree code. Everything else is blown out of water."

So far no jurisdiction has actually triggered the Builder's Remedy, with Carnation getting fully into compliance earlier this summer, and Bainbridge Island going the same route as Beaux Arts and approving a temporary ordinance a few days after Carnation. But in Beaux Arts just as there was on Bainbridge Island, some voices pushed for a more oppositional stance against state review.
During Tuesday's public hearing, local resident Dan Bridges urged councilmembers to take a more adversarial position.

"Well-meaning councils and boards sometimes lose sight of the fact that public agencies, state agencies – who we trust, like our parents, right? – they're still political agencies, and they have an agenda and they have a point of view. That point of view is not always the correct point of view," Bridges said. "Having an outside [entity] of coming to advocate for us would be helpful. And I would suggest if you haven't done that yet, you might consider doing that and not simply accept what some state agency is telling you. Only a judge is the one who decides the law."
For now at least, Beaux Arts Village has deemed the path of least resistance to be compliance.

"It is not that we are not receptive of what we're hearing," Stowe told public commenters. "It's that we quite frankly are up against them to comply, or they're going to go over us and say you have no authority and allow whatever zoning or buildings they say under the code – under Commerce's interpretation of the code, which has not necessarily been ours – and we have pointed that out that we don't read the law the same way they do."
As one of the first jurisdictions being put under the Housing Accountability Act microscope, Beaux Arts officials expressed clear frustration at the process of state review over the past few months.

They're not alone in that frustration. When members of the Carnation City Council held a public hearing with the Department of Commerce in July, many of the same concerns raised in Beaux Arts surfaced – about staff time, not an insignificant issue for a small city or town, and confusion over the purpose of the new law.

"Is this supposed to be helpful for us?," Carnation deputy Mayor Jessica Merizan asked Commerce staff at that July 9 meeting. "Because it really seems like you've pulled a lot of staff time, and the point seems to be saving staff time because these types of errors are happening. It just kind of feels like this is a teacher double-checking work, and not necessarily, these are areas of the community, in the region that perhaps need support, and we're here to offer that."

In Beaux Arts Village, Howes directly referred to what the Commerce department had been tasked with doing as "overreach" and called the idea of the state forcing local officials to spend scarce staff time on that review as an "unfunded mandate" that she called "bullshit."

"I am still pursuing the legislative changes in the next session with [Representative] Zahn, [Representative Thai], and [the Association of Washington Cities] is still pushing the seven legal arguments that we brought to them, and the seven other cities are also pushing to get those changes," Howes said, noting the temporary ordinance's four-month duration. "So if something moves during that time frame, then we can amend. If something doesn't move and it goes to final...you know, we'll see how the legislative session goes in '27."

Meanwhile, five additional cities and towns – including Woodway, Darrington, Gold Bar, Brier, and DuPont – are still in the process of coming into compliance, work that was spurred on by the Housing Accountability Act. And then next year, a whole new slate of jurisdictions will be announced.

articles.title: Central District House: Seattle’s first ground-up Social Housing project will rise at 24th and Yesler
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: The Bird’s modernist angles will make way for 20 new affordable homes (Image: Seattle Dream Homes )
The first new affordable building the Seattle Social Housing Developer builds from the ground up will come in the Central District.

The Seattle Social Housing Developer has announced Central District House , its first construction project, will take place at 2402 E Yesler Way, marking a major milestone for the public development authority.

Plans call for a roughly $15 million, 20-home mixed-income development designed to Passive House environmental standards, with over half configured as two- and three-bedroom family units. Tenant selection will prioritize Central District residents and “people with current and historical roots” through the city’s Community Preference guidelines to help counter displacement.
Atelierjones is attached as the architect for the project.
The 20 new homes will be affordable rental units, permanently owned and operated by the public development authority.
SSHD has been making steady progress since its approval by the city’s voters in 2023.
CHS reported last winter on stronger than expected funding for the new authority giving the developer a head start in its mission to create and acquire affordable housing.

Officials said the voter-approved 5% tax on employers that pay any employee more than $1 million in compensation climbed above $115 million. The city began collecting the first Prop 1A payments from employers for the 2025 tax year in January. The tax had been expected to raise more than $50 million annually. A reported “10,000 applicants” signed up for the lottery for the developer’s first acquired property on Western Ave.

The income mix in Seattle Social Housing Developer properties is hoped to differ from previous affordable housing in Seattle by using mixed-income tier structure that spans from deeply low-income households up to middle-income earners, rather than serving low-income tenants exclusively.

The Central District and Capitol Hill have absorbed a large portion of the city’s most recent waves of redevelopment. In addition to market rate projects, major affordable redevelopment has reshaped many blocks.
The opening of Community Roots Housing’s Liberty Bank Building at 24th and Union in 2019 created 115 100%-affordable apartment units and street level commercial and restaurant space.
The Africatown Plaza mixed-use building at 23rd and Spring opened in 2025 as a 100% affordable, publicly funded project from Africatown Community Land Trust and Community Roots.

Meanwhile, developer Jaebadiah Gardner has held up his efforts with former church properties along 23rd Ave as examples a for-profit response can be part of balancing the city’s need for new housing with equitable growth in the Central District.
Other for-profit developments are also reshaping the area including the seven-story Acer House , the new “Afrofuturist”-styled development at the corner of 23rd and Cherry.
SSHD’s mission to serve the city will begin a few blocks east but its plans stretch beyond the CD.

Interim Chief Executive Officer Tiffani McCoy said the authority expects to announce a second acquisition before the end of year. By the end of 2027, SSHD plans to own more than 1,000 homes. “The ambitious pipeline is dependent on a successful low-interest bond issuance,” the authority said in its announcement.

The Central District corner has civic roots. it holds two cabin-like structures built by the late Washington State House Speaker Frank Chopp and his father, including “The Portal” and “The Bird,” a timber-framed home where Chopp’s daughter and community members lived. As the story goes, Chopp and his father bought the land at a public auction to build the structures as “ sort of a de facto Eagle Scout project .” The structures weren’t completed until the early 1980s.
Following Chopp’s passing in 2025, his widow, Nancy Long , offered the site to SSHD to advance his legacy as an affordable housing champion .
The property, just around the corner from the Douglass-Truth Library , is valued at $940,000, according to the county.
The modernist — but poorly aged — structures will be demolished to make way for the new building.
SSHD staff confirmed feasibility studies showed the 0.18-acre parcel is “very suitable for a Seattle social housing development with minimal risks to construction.”

During Thursday’s board vote, member Carl Nelson praised the deeper impact on residents: “A budget is an ethical decision, and the power to change that with your neighbors… I just want to commend the staff for what I think are really exciting first steps.”
Groundbreaking is scheduled for fall 2027, with completion targeted by late 2028.

articles.title: Interim chief’s punishment for ‘here to fuck people up’ Cal Anderson protest cop? Written reprimand
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: The Seattle Police lieutenant caught on video rallying cops with a “here to fuck people up” pep speech during a May 2025 demonstration at Cal Anderson Park has been punished with a written reprimand.

Interim Chief Andre Sayles issued the reprimand to Lieutenant Matthew Didier over his inappropriate language captured on body-worn video as SPD prepared to move in on demonstrators against an anti-trans Christian group’s rally.
“We are past talking to people,” Didier says at one point in the video. “We’re here to fuck people up now. We’re done with these guys and the shit they’re doing.”

“Leaders set the tone for those they lead. Words spoken before officers enter a crowd shape how that crowd is policed,” Interim Chief Andre Sayles said Friday in a statement on the reprimand that followed the Office of Police Accountability upholding a complaint filed against Didier.

CHS reported here on the May 2025 #DontMessWithOurKids gathering in Cal Anderson and the more than 20 people arrested during protests against the anti-trans rally as a large battalion of Seattle Police armed with batons and pepper spray moved in.
The Cal Anderson crackdown was an early dent in the leadership under then- Chief Shon Barnes .

Findings from a Seattle Office of Inspector General report concluded SPD was ignorant “of the broader cultural and political context of the rally and location” in its heavy handed response to the counter demonstration.
Now, a year and a half after the incident, Sayles explained the discipline adhered to disciplinary guidelines following sustained findings by the Office of Police Accountability.

Because Didier is a supervisor represented by the Seattle Police Management Association , his discipline had to follow union-mandated progressive discipline and meet arbitration standards for just cause. Factoring in Didier’s prior record, the Office of Police Accountability’s recommended penalty range ran from an oral reprimand to a two-day suspension .

The Sayles statement also addressed the Office of Inspector General review, acknowledging that police actions during the rally damaged trust with Seattle’s LGBTQ+ community. In the statement, the interim chief pledged to reform crowd management policies, adopt oversight recommendations, and engage local community groups directly ahead of future events.
Mayor Katie Wilson’s search for new Seattle Police chief launched in August with an advisory committee, online survey for public priorities, and a “$234,294.48 – $374,900.40” salary range.
The recruitment follows a turbulent period after the removal of Barnes amid fallout from a deadly Seattle Center shootout, leaving Sayles currently at the helm.

articles.title: Mattress fire knocked down by sprinkler system at 16th and Howell
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Seattle Fire mounted a full response to a fire at 16th and Howell Sunday night but the blaze was handled by the building’s sprinkler system.
According to SFD, the fire in the assisted living apartment building was reported at 9:15 PM.
Crews reported the incident as a mattress fire brought under control by the building’s fire suppression system.
Damage was limited and there were no reported injuries.

articles.title: How a Family-Owned Business in the South End Turns Food Scraps Into Compost
paras: Each week, many King County residents participate in a ritual: They take bags of food scraps to the green waste dumpster or roll their compost bin to the curb. About 18 months later, the banana peels and apple cores that were thrown in the compost will be the ingredients in a bag of Cedar Grove compost. Cedar Grove, which processes much of King County's green waste into compost at a site in Maple Valley, is roughly 30 minutes from Rainier Beach. Its headquarters are in Georgetown.

"I'm in a third-generation family business," said Stephan Banchero III, president of Cedar Grove. His grandparents were Italian immigrants who settled in Beacon Hill's established Italian immigrant neighborhood in the early 1900s. In the 1930s, "garbage was not a very lucrative business, and nobody wanted to pick it up, so the Italians got together and created a company to collect it," said Banchero. His grandfather, John Banchero Sr., along with Alfonso Morelli and Josie Razore, founded Seattle Disposal in 1938, a company that spun off other companies, like Rabanco (Razore-Banchero Company). Banchero grew up with the industry all around him. His father, Stephan Banchero Jr., is Cedar Grove's CEO.
In the 1980s, as Seattle worked toward decreasing the amount of garbage sent to landfills, the City approached the company to start a composting program for residential yard waste.

"The City said they'd bring 5,000 tons of yard waste to the property, [which] our grandparents purchased in Maple Valley," said Banchero. "They arrived with 50,000 tons of yard waste from residents in 1988." Banchero's father and his team traveled throughout the country and Europe to study the best available control technology for composting. In 2008, Cedar Grove began taking non-cooked vegetative scraps. In 2011, the company began taking all food waste, including cooked foods and meats.

In 2022, Washington State passed the Plastic Product Degradability Act, which required certification and proper labeling of compostable food service products, like cups, plates, and to-go containers. "Words like 'biodegradable' and 'degradable' on an item don't mean it can be placed in the compost bin," said Jay Blazey, Cedar Grove general counsel. Certified compostable products now have green, beige, or brown markings and include a certification stamp.
Currently, the Maple Valley site receives more than 200,000 tons of raw material, known as "feedstock," a year, which it turns into roughly 100,000 tons of compost.
Here's what happens to tons and tons of kitchen scraps and yard waste.

First stop for food scraps is the tipping building, where green waste is "tipped" out of trucks. Gabe Morelli, Cedar Grove Maple Valley operations manager, can watch what comes in on a monitor from his office. In the photo above, Morelli takes larger contaminants out of the feedstock that just arrived at the site.

About 80% of the feedstock is from residential contributions, and feedstock, from any source, can contain contaminants, including plastic bags, plastic bottles, and plastic gloves. Sometimes people put their garbage in the compost, which needs to be removed. Cedar Grove doesn't accept glass because it's a safety risk in compost material. Pet feces is a pathogen risk and isn't allowed in compost bins. "Contamination is a problem," said Banchero "[The compost] is only as good as the material that you receive."

Cedar Grove adds carbon and water to raw feedstock material and, if needed, nitrogen. The feedstock is piled into mounds where it sits covered with an inch of organic composting byproduct for about 20 days. This cover insulates the pile, mitigates odor, and detracts rats, seagulls, and other animals.

After about 20 days, the material heads down a covered conveyor belt to "the pie," an area of partially decomposed mounds that are shaped like pie wedges. This area operates with an air-circulation system that captures the smells and ammonia emitted by the feedstock. The material is aerated in the pie for about another 40 days.

Compost sites like Cedar Grove are regulated by multiple levels of government. Inspectors routinely test for odors and check filters, maintenance, water-management practices, and more. Each month, a sample of finished compost material is tested by a third-party lab for pathogens, heavy metals, and inert materials, like plastic.

Cedar Grove uses another alternative compost-processing method at Maple Valley for the first 60 days called the Gore cover system, where feedstock is covered with a specialized cloth and the temperature and oxygen in the system are managed with fans.

The feedstock then moves from the pie to the "kraken," where the material is sifted through a screening system. The kraken uses magnets to remove metal, while more than 20 suction heads vacuum out plastic film.

Nick Blanchette, Cedar Grove Maple Valley facility manager, says the composted material is separated into three categories, based on size: large organic matter, like stubs of branches; inch-long bits; and fine material called "fines." Fines are sent to mounds that cure for 12 to 18 months. The oversized material can be ground up or used as cover for new feedstock.

After the fines finish curing, they're sifted once more and become finished compost. The majority is used by public agencies, some of which mix it with sand for landscaping projects. A portion is bagged to sell in stores for people to amend garden soil.

Morelli said he's moved by working with a process that doesn't waste anything. "If you work in sand, gravel, and rock quarry, there's always a waste product," he said. Morelli described how all organic matter that's too big to be composted is recycled back into the system to break down more. "We're micro-farmers. All we really do is add air and water. We screen it, we size it, and Mother Nature does the rest. Then we put it back."

articles.title: The Oatmeal and His Brother Built Jimothy’s Evil Dad to Haunt Bainbridge Island This Halloween
articles.author: Cedar Attanasio
paras: Sifting through the infosphere as I drafted Monday’s Slog AM, I was delighted to stumble on an Instagram post introducing Grimothy aka “Jim Reaper, Dark Lord and Father of Jimothy,” as his creators call him. Could this monstrosity have sown Seattle’s favorite short-spined raccoon whose likeness has been co-opted by sports teams, artisanal cutting boards, and the ugliest t-shirts known to man?

Grimothy, the broader-than-human-sized raccoon, is an animatronic Halloween installation. He is ghastly, but also beautiful. His red eyes glow, his bony arms flail—as if grasping toward Ballard, the hellscape his son has run off to—and his mouth of spiky teeth chomp towards cars and pedestrians in a quiet corner of Bainbridge Island.

This DIY freakshow (sorry, Grimothy) is the brainchild of brothers Matt and Bryce Inman. You may recognize Matt’s flair on Grimothy’s, um, essence. Matt is the cartoonist behind the card game Exploding Kittens and the webcomic The Oatmeal . Grimothy, while surely a haunted demon, bears a striking resemblance to Matt’s cute, but depraved style. Grimothy is currently living and snarling along Bryce’s sidewalk across from Cherry Avenue across from the Wing Point Golf & Country Club.
I had to know more. How did they put this together? Are they ready for a million visitors?

Inman told me in an email that he and his brother, Bryce, welded, wired, and “servoed” this monstrosity to something resembling life. I’ve reconstituted his responses, from him and his brother, below.
Is your brother ready for some foot traffic?
Matt: Last night (Saturday) at around 9:30 p.m., there was still a line of cars outside the house. We realized we’d turned the front yard into an all-hours tourist attraction.
What was the toughest part about building this?

Bryce : Getting the main ring structure welded together was tough because some steel rods are small and anything more than a tiny spot weld burns through and cuts the piece in half. So, if I made one small mistake Jimothy would implode on top of me. Also, the rag I used to clean the welder kept catching fire because of all the flying sparks, and Grimothy’s fur is super flammable. So generally speaking implosions and explosions were the hardest part.

Matt: Learning to work with servos—they are like little motors that make things move. Since my electrical skills are non-existent, Grimothy’s interior is a total hack job of bad wiring and electrical tape. Every few hours Grimothy has the robot equivalent of a stroke and half his face stops working. I then have to crawl inside him through a flap near the butt and jiggle a bunch of cables. It’s like an animatronic colonoscopy.

Matt: I directed my first short film, which debuted at film festivals across the country this year. It’s called My Dog: The Paradox , and it won Best Animated Comedy at the Portland Festival of Cinema and Animation. Other than that, I’m writing an all-ages science book that covers topics like neuroscience, black holes, wombat butts, and the mantis shrimp.
But mostly I’ve been spending time with my brother crawling in and out of a massive raccoon ass.

articles.title: Stranger Suggests: Your Agenda This Week, October 19–25
articles.author: Julianne Bell, Amanda Manitach, Dave Segal, and Audrey Vann
paras: (LITERATURE) What can’t Barbara Kingsolver do? The bestselling author never misses, from her historical fiction classic The Poisonwood Bible to her 2022 Pulitzer Prize-winning sensation Demon Copperhead . Her most recent novel, Partita , follows piano teacher Livia Cable, who lives a peaceful, unassuming married life in the Tennessee countryside until an unexpected call from her ex-lover dredges up memories of trauma, tragedy, and her abandoned ambitions for a musical career. The book borrows both its name and format from a musical composition made up of dance movements. See Kingsolver discuss her lyrical work, her writing process, and the connection between art and life at Benaroya Hall, and don’t forget to bring donations for Ballard Food Bank’s food drive in the lobby, such as boxed mac and cheese, ramen, granola bars, oatmeal packets, cereal, and jerky. ( Benaroya Hall, 7:30 pm, all ages ) JULIANNE BELL

(MUSIC) The son of legendary experimental saxophonist Anthony Braxton, Tyondai’s anything but a nepo baby. He’s earned his lofty status in underground music through his exploits in former best band in the omniverse Battles, who took math rock to rarely matched realms of rhythmic complexity, melodic whimsicality, and electronic tomfoolery. Braxton departed Battles in 2010 and since then has been focusing on a solo career that’s veered from vaulting orchestral and electroacoustic composition to abstract electronic music that could discombobulate Autechre fans’ neurons. On Braxton’s mind-bending new album, Splayed Werks , he conjures alien sound worlds that expand the vocabulary of electronic-music composition. This is a rare seated show at Vera, so STFU and listen. ( Vera Project, 7 pm, all ages ) DAVE SEGAL

(MUSIC) Astute local music critic and DJ Martin Douglas has coordinated another strong bill for his Trick Bag series. Olympia’s premier experimental-rock band, Debt Rag, puts punk and no wave in a cyclotron, resulting in concise, idiosyncratic songs that send diabolical heat and sparks through your sensorium. The trio’s music and lyrics possess the urgency and righteous rage that this perilous timeline demands. Check out their latest album, It Is Clear What’s Going On , for proof. Seattle’s Miscomings seemingly have absorbed the harsh lessons of the legendary No New York comp and transformed them into tracks that come at you like a herd of amphetamine-spiked porcupines, with bonus doses of Minutemen-like funk. Exhilaration awaits you. ( Sunset Tavern, 8 pm, 21+ ) DAVE SEGAL
MOPOP’s Icons of Pop Culture Gala With Salt-N-Pepa

(MUSIC) MOPOP’s Icons of Pop Culture Gala is probably your only chance to see the queens of hip-hop, Salt-N-Pepa, at a venue this tiny (unless you time-travel back to 1986). The duo, with DJ Spinderella, of course, will perform classics like “Whatta Man,” “Shoop,” “Let’s Talk About Sex,” and “None of Your Business” at the 250-capacity Sky Church. I really hope they also play a few songs from their criminally underrated 1997 album Brand New , which is rich with wordplay and glossy ’90s production, in the same vein as Lil’ Kim’s Hard Core . And look, I recognize that the $250 ticket price is no small thing, but if you’ve ever paid Ticketmaster/Live Nation hundreds of dollars, don’t think twice about supporting the MOPOP with their future exhibitions, youth education programs, and community initiatives. ( MOPOP, 8:30 pm, 21+ ) AUDREY VANN

(VISUAL ART) Melissa Messer describes her practice and work as “if Rothko’s daughter were obsessed with form.” I might add Albers to the mix: her approach to color is technical and clever and makes the eyeballs vibrate with a kind of ocular orgasm. But she’s right about Rothko, because her use of hue is almost spiritual in its ability to overwhelm. She is also a preeminent figurative painter, using the human body as an armature upon which to drape shades of deciduous greens, burnt orange, and acid gold. Beneath all that color, however, the figures hold their own. Messer paints to convey intimacy—the kind that comes from knowing the closeness of a body from innumerable hours of holding, caring, carrying, or resting. That feeling is palpable in the heavy limbs of the mothers, friends, and others who populate her canvases. They loom, stark and monumental, bodies dissolving into the color fields that surround them. ( Spectrum Fine Art, 12–5 pm ) AMANDA MANITACH
Mourning Sickness: ‘Elvira: Mistress of the Dark’

(FILM) Until recently, I had never seen Elvira: Mistress of the Dark , but rest assured I am making up for lost time. The 1988 cult classic revolves around everyone’s favorite goth horror hostess, Elvira (played by the iconic Cassandra Gay Peterson), who discovers her great-aunt Morgana bequeathed her a crumbling mansion in a small-minded town named Fallwell (likely a reference to conservative televangelist Jerry Falwell). The result is a delightful fish-out-of-water story, featuring relentless innuendos, a pink-dyed poodle named Gonk, a himbo love interest, a villain named Chastity Pariah, Tic Tac pie, and a bacchanalian picnic scene. This film was made in a lab for the gays—the slut-shaming and moral panic of the townspeople; Elvira’s fabulous drag; the film’s dedication to Peterson’s late best friend and makeup artist Robert Allen Redding, who died of AIDS; and of course, the fact that Peterson herself is sexually fluid and has been living her best queer life in Portland with her partner of 24 years, Teresa “T” Wierson. Who better to present this campy masterpiece than local queen Monday Mourning? ( Northwest Film Forum, 8 pm, all ages ) JULIANNE BELL

(MUSIC) Ken Ishii was the first Japanese solo electronic-music producer I got hip to, thanks to his 1995 album Flare dazzling me with its ingenious textures and dynamic rhythms. Throughout the ’90s, Ishii released a grip of phenomenal records in which IDM, techno, funky breaks, and ambient converged into fascinating hybrids. Shamefully, I lost track of him in the ’00s, but, whoa, Ken’s still creating and DJing like a madman, including a 2019 collab with Detroit techno legend Jeff Mills. Whether he’s performing his own cuts or spinning others’ in his wide-ranging sets, Ishii manifests a distinctive brand of dance-floor hypnosis. At Substation, he’ll be DJing, along with Cory Simpson, a prime mover in Seattle’s techno scene who heads the Depth crew. ( Substation, 7 pm, 21+ ) DAVE SEGAL

articles.title: Slog AM: Seattleites March, Israel Spins Settler Attack, Bainbridge Brothers Win Halloween
articles.author: Cedar Attanasio
paras: Good morning and happy Monday to those who celebrate.

Envelopes with suspicious white powder have been sent to congressional offices ahead of the midterms, NBC reports . US Rep. Pramila Jayapal’s staff evacuated her Seattle office Friday afternoon after a similar package was found in the mailroom. It turned out to be nothing physically dangerous, The Seattle Times reported . Another letter was intercepted on its way to the state Secretary of State’s office in Olympia, KOMO reports . A similar terrorist attack happened in 2023, and the culprit was never found.

Speaking of terrorism, US officials denounced Israeli settlers’ attacks on an American journalist, a French mayor, and others over the weekend. The New York Times reports Bibi Netanyahu’s heavy spin on the assaults, which left an American photographer with broken ribs and vertebrae while she was photographing the Palestinian olive harvest. On Saturday US Secretary of State Marco Rubio offered this tepid response: “We’ve asked the Israelis and continue to ask them to crack down on that stuff,” and defended Trump’s lifting of Biden’s sanctions against Israeli settlers.

Ten Israelis arrested in connection with the attack: Al Jazeera reports that Israeli police arrested 10 people in connection with acts of violence, violating a closed military zone, and illegal construction. Well look at that! The Israeli army can crack down on settler violence when it wants to . They earned an “attaboy” from ardent Zionist and US ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee. In the past, he’s suggested deporting Palestinians from their land to neighboring Muslim nations, to free up more land for Israeli settlers.
Trump endorsed Netanyahu, a first in US-Israel relations, Axios reports , despite misgivings behind the scenes.

“Trump is using his power to intimidate the people who run our elections,” CBS reports. Lesley Stahl broke down the efforts on a sharp 60 Minutes segment, which looks at the series of authoritarian power grabs across the US. For example, on Friday, Trump threatened California officials with prison time if they counted certain mail ballots over unsubstantiated voter fraud claims.

Paris police arrested 855 of the more than 110,000 people who were out protesting in the city, calling for better education investments, ABC reports . That’s more than the 600ish protesters arrested during the entire 1999 Seattle WTO protests.

Two women on opposite sides of Seattle’s 1999 WTO protests have died in the past month, the Seattle Times reports. Social justice Organizer KL Shannon died last month at 59. Born in Albuquerque, New Mexico (shoutout to my 505ers), Shannon was remembered as a “warrior” by political leaders in Seattle who first met her as she protested and organized during the WTO protests. Pat Davis, then-director of the Port of Seattle, died earlier this month. She’s credited for inviting the WTO to Seattle . She was 91.

What happened to the WTO? The World Trade Organization was neutered by Trump, ignored by Biden, and basically doesn’t do anything anymore. The WTO used to adjudicate disputes over tariffs. But now it’s withering away . Trump defunded the organization, and deprived the body’s appeals court of a quorum by blocking appointments .

Nobody was arrested at the No Kings rally over the weekend . SPD told KIRO that, unlike in Portland —where protesters broke off from the main rally to attack the gate at an ICE facility — nobody ended up in the clink. The main message of the rally was VOTE EARLY IN THE MIDTERMS. Not registered to vote? There’s still time to register and vote in this election in person or online .

A Halloween installation in Bainbridge depicts Jimothy’s evil father, Grimothy . Co-creator Matt Inman, a cartoonist best known for the game Exploding Kittens and the webcomic The Oatmeal , posted the monstrosity on his Instagram over the weekend. It’s a human-height furry raccoon animatron with glowing red eyes, flailing bony arms, and a chomping and a crooked-toothed mandible. Inman told me in an email that he and his brother, Bryce, welded, wired, and “servoed” this monstrosity to something resembling life. Grimothy is on display at his brother’s house, on Cherry Avenue across from the Wing Point Golf & Country Club. Inman says it’s turned the neighborhood into a 24/7 tourist destination.

A grass fire that started at a Canadian military base got out of control and led to four deaths and dozens of injuries. The Associated Press reports that Canadian officials were still determining what sparked the fire on Saturday, during grenade-throwing exercises. Canada Prime Minister Mark Carney described it as one of the worst peace-time military tragedies on Canadian soil. (The worst Canadian military tragedy happened in Halifax, during World War I when a French ship filled with explosives collided with another ship and exploded, killing 1,782 and injuring an estimated 9,000).

Students in Bend, Oregon, are going back to school this week for the first time since the mass shooting there. Three children and a teacher were killed by a 16-year-old with a shotgun on Thursday, and Oregon Public Broadcasting reports parents are bracing for the emotional strain of dropping their kids off there on Wednesday. The shooter was killed by a “ good guy with a gun .” The shooter reportedly got the shotgun from his mom , who could face charges depending on how the investigation plays out.

Love Em or hate ‘em: Detroit’s Kid Rock and Eminem have teamed up in a pre-midterm show of solidarity, Rolling Stone reports . Their new song “Heal My Faith” is the lyrical equivalent of an unexpected animal friendship video, with Eminem’s signature inventive style recounting the duo’s bond as Detroit natives. Eminem endorsed Kamala Harris for president in 2024 and has been critical of Trump. He says guesting on Kid Rock’s track was about making music, “not about choosing sides.” Rock’s verse, in my reading, subconsciously charts his own journey from saying “ fuck off ” to embracing Trump and authoritarianism.
‘Cause it’s time to bear witness, take the path of least resistance
Bow your head, hey, and pray for forgiveness
Why evil exists and what it does to good men

‘ Eminem, do you have that video of my friend’s boobs on the Interstate? Mr. Mathers, let me take you back to 2002, north of Albuquerque, New Mexico, on Interstate 25. You were riding in the red Anger Management Tour bus when we passed you in a sedan. My friend’s girlfriend maneuvered at around 75 miles per hour in front of your tour bus, where Bizarre was up front talking with the diver. One of the adult women in our sedan managed to open the sunroof, stand up, and bare her breasts into the headlights of the tour bus. Somebody on the bus (Obie Trice maybe?) was holding a camcorder, and we think we remember you checking out the action. I think of that high-speed stunt and wonder if those boobs are archived in your agent’s basement or the Library of Congress, along with my dumb teenage face starting out the rear window.
Here’s the Detroit stop of that Anger Management Tour. It was a circus.

articles.title: Secrets, lies and a shock A-list cameo: how You Can See Everything became the film of the year
articles.author: Adrian Horton
paras: Nathan Fielder’s secretive Elizabeth Holmes documentary has become a sold-out smash hit and might make Oscars history

If there is one moment that sums up You Can See Everything , the new A24 documentary on Elizabeth Holmes that until this weekend was shrouded in spoiler-averse secrecy, it is, perhaps surprisingly, the one everyone already knows: co-director Nathan Fielder, the droll comedian known for deadpanning subjects into submission, sitting eye to eye with Holmes, the unblinking fabulist of Theranos infamy. In tight zoom, saturation turned up – Fielder’s arched brows and Holmes’s oceanic blue eyes as stark as two magnetic poles – he asks her: “Are you being real right now?”

That question hangs over much of the colossal three-hour movie, particularly a claustrophobic first half that has made headlines since the film’s existence was announced in September. That first half – essentially, the only part of the movie anyone respecting spoiler guidelines and/or the theatrical experience could talk about – takes place entirely in 2023, when Fielder and his co-director Lance Oppenheim, along with a small crew, embedded with Holmes, her husband, Billy Evans, and their two small children in the run-up to her prison sentence for fraud. We watch as Fielder, over a few surreal weeks in a beachfront rental, attempts to puncture Holmes’s indomitable facade of faultlessness. It’s not exactly comedic, this chess game between three norms-ignoring people, but it can be quite funny: TV’s grand illusionist, an absurdist auteur who will go as far as actually obtaining a 737 pilot’s license for the bit, stymied by a world-class fabricator, with her poorly dissembling husband on the side. This section resembles, in feel, the pull of an internet wormhole: the closer you zoom in on a subject, without outside context, the more sense devolves. Was Holmes “being real”, for instance, when she told Fielder, with seemingly complete sincerity, that she has never told a lie in her life ? Or when she continued to insist, despite plain reality, that Theranos devices could perform 1,000 diagnostic tests?

articles.title: ‘They pulled a guy’s face off. It’s my favourite bit!’ Linda Cardellini on Freaks and Geeks, Mad Men and slasher horror Crystal Lake
articles.author: Rebecca Nicholson
paras: She got to torment Don Draper in Mad Men and has just won an Emmy for DTF St Louis. But nothing prepared the star for all the gore as she switched to horror with the Friday the 13th prequel

‘The first time I had the tooth in my hand,” says Linda Cardellini, “I thought, ‘Oh my God, this is what I’m doing.’” The star of Freaks and Geeks, ER, Dead to Me, Mad Men and DTF St Louis (for which she recently won an Emmy) is talking about her pivot towards full-blown horror. In Crystal Lake, the prequel to the Friday the 13th movies, Cardellini plays Pamela Voorhees, the original slasher of the 1980 film. The tooth, by the way, is human and gets embedded in Pam’s knuckle – until she yanks it out with a gruesome, revolting slurping sound.

Casual filmgoers may associate Friday the 13th with Jason, the hockey-mask-wearing serial killer. But aficionados will know that Pam, Jason’s mother, is the villain of the first movie. “He didn’t even have the mask until the third movie,” says Cardellini, who has clearly done her homework. “Pam is the original killer, in vengeance of his death.” (There is some massaging of previous storylines in Crystal Lake, such as moving Jason’s drowning from the 1950s to the early 70s, but since the franchise is flexible enough to have sent Jason into space at one point, a bit of timeline tweaking feels fair game.)

For years, Saudi Arabia’s crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, cultivated a close relationship with Donald Trump and his son-in-law and former top adviser, Jared Kushner. The prince understood the president’s transactional approach to power: he signed deals to buy billions of dollars’ worth of US weapons and invested billions more in American companies.

Days after Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, Prince Mohammed pledged to expand investment and trade with the US by $600bn over four years. He later promised to increase that investment to nearly $1tn, although it wasn’t entirely clear how Saudi Arabia would manage to plough a sum close to the kingdom’s entire annual GDP into a foreign economy over a few years.

articles.title: Federal spending on climate change before 2024 election boosted incumbents of both parties
articles.author:
<name>Kayla Morton, Assistant Professor of Blue Economy and Policy, University of Delaware</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/kayla-morton-2765157"/>
paras: A massive federal spending effort to combat climate change passed in 2022 without a single Republican vote in the U.S. House or the Senate . But the billions of dollars it authorized benefited Republican and Democratic politicians alike – so long as they were already in the House of Representatives – according to an analysis I conducted with several fellow researchers. The results suggest that incumbents can still reap electoral rewards when federal money reaches their districts, even if they opposed the bill that provided it.

Enacted in 2022, the Inflation Reduction Act squeaked through the Senate only through a tiebreaking vote cast by Vice President Kamala Harris . It authorized spending US$370 billion to combat climate change and lower greenhouse gas emissions , primarily through subsidies such as a tax credit of up to $7,500 for buying an electric vehicle and incentives for making commercial buildings more energy efficient , rather than by imposing new fees or taxes.
Before the 2024 election, over $204 billion had been spent on clean energy projects around the country, through a combination of private investment and federal incentives.
While Republicans opposed the legislation, 79% of the law’s investment went to Republican congressional districts.

Even when Republicans vote against climate legislation at the national level, at least some favor investing in clean energy technology at the state and local level, because those investments bring local economic benefits. Many Republican districts, which are often large and more rural, are well suited to these kinds of projects.

Elected officials are sometimes accused of “ pork barrel politics ,” seeking to direct federal taxpayer spending to their own congressional districts. In part that’s because voters see federal investment as creating local jobs and stimulating economic growth.

Although no Republican voted for the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022, some Republican lawmakers began defending parts of the law as investments reached their districts. In August 2024, heading into the election, 18 Republican House members urged House Speaker Mike Johnson to preserve the law’s clean energy tax credits, which they said “created good jobs in many parts of the country – including many districts represented by members of our conference.”

That support continued after the election. In March 2025, after Republicans retained control of the House and party leaders began considering cuts to the law’s programs, even more Republican House members called for preserving the clean energy tax credits, which could be used, for example, to finance a large wind energy project or construction of a battery factory. The lawmakers argued that repealing the credits while major projects were still under construction would jeopardize investments already underway and the jobs tied to them.
Our analysis finds that Inflation Reduction Act funding helped incumbent House members of both parties in the 2024 election.

During the campaign, both Democrats and Republicans highlighted benefits of the investments funded by the act. Republicans usually used language like “ economic development opportunities ,” while Democrats directly mentioned the act itself.

Some districts got nothing, and one got nearly $8 billion. Some of the largest investments were in Republican-held districts in North Carolina and Georgia to expand capacity at electric vehicle plants already under construction. These companies were eligible for corporate tax breaks from the law and hoped to benefit from increased consumer demand because of the law’s tax credit for people purchasing electric vehicles.

In Mississippi’s 2nd Congressional District, which got $588 million in funding from the Inflation Reduction Act, Rep. Bennie Thompson, a Democrat, received 61.8% of the vote in 2024, up from 60% in 2022. In Michigan’s 5th District, which got almost $2 billion under the law, Rep. Tim Walberg, a Republican, received 65.7% of the vote in 2024, up from 62% in 2022.
We found that the more money a representative’s district got from the Inflation Reduction Act, the more the candidate improved their electoral performance in 2024 over how they had done in 2022.

When we conducted our statistical analysis, we accounted for multiple factors that could influence election results, including the district’s support for Trump, the incumbent’s previous vote share, campaign spending and district demographics. Using statistical methods to isolate the effects of Inflation Reduction Act funding, we found that doubling the amount of federal investment in a congressional district led to about a 0.9 percentage-point increase in the incumbent’s 2024 vote share relative to their 2022 result.

Our analysis showed that both Democratic and Republican incumbents saw electoral benefits from Inflation Reduction Act investment, even though Republicans in Congress had universally opposed the legislation. While some incumbents still lost votes or their seats, the data showed that greater Inflation Reduction Act investment helped them perform better than they otherwise would have.
These results indicate that voters may respond more to the money coming into their districts than to the underlying purpose of that funding.

While previous federal spending projects helped incumbent House members in elections , we found no direct evidence that district economies improved between 2022 and 2024. Instead, it’s more likely that incumbents claiming credit for the investments on the campaign trail explained why election results improved with Inflation Reduction Act funding. The lesson is that voters pay attention to actual or promised investments that might come into their areas.

Upon taking office in 2025, the Trump administration and the Republican majority in the House rolled back many of the law’s climate provisions . A massive package of tax breaks and spending cuts sometimes referred to as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” removed tax credits for energy efficiency improvements and electric vehicle purchases.
The Trump administration has also moved to expand fossil fuel production on federal lands.

This evidence indicates that presidential priorities can outweigh even direct benefits to House members on highly polarized issues. The fact that some climate-related tax credits remained even after passage of the big budget bill does indicate that economic development policies may remain appealing to Republican leadership.

These electoral benefits indicate voters may reward investments even when the policies that created them remain politically contentious. Economic investments in fighting climate change can generate local political benefits across party lines, even if those benefits are not enough to overcome national divisions over climate change.
