articles.title: A pregnant mom let her 5-year-old stay outside to collect goose feathers – and was placed on the child abuse and neglect registry
articles.author:
<name>Jennifer L. Brinkley, Assistant Professor of Law, University of Dayton</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/jennifer-l-brinkley-2760391"/>
paras: Ford’s Colony in Williamsburg is a leafy, gated community in Virginia’s colonial-era historic region with 10 miles of trails and 24-hour security.

On June 5, 2026, Karyann Parkinson, a recent law school graduate pregnant with her fifth child, was on a walk through their neighborhood in Ford’s Colony with her 5-year-old son. On their way home, her son asked if he could collect a few goose feathers at a nearby pond. She said yes, confident in his ability to walk there and back safely.

About 20 minutes later, a security guard from Ford’s Colony knocked on her door, with her son by his side. He explained that a neighbor had seen the child walking by himself, and that he was going to call the police to report her. Within an hour, law enforcement and child protective services were at Parkinson’s door to inform her that they were investigating her for neglect .

After being placed on the child abuse and neglect registry for lack of supervision , Parkinson was convicted of contributing to the delinquency of a minor and received a six-month suspended jail sentence. Parkinson has appealed to the Circuit Court and will have a jury trial in 2027.

I stumbled upon Parkinson’s case while researching and writing a law review article about states that are trying to encourage childhood independence by lessening penalties on parents who allow their children to play outdoors while unsupervised. Virginia, ironically, is one of those states.
Parkinson’s experience is not unique. In my scholarship and in my work as a family lawyer, I’ve seen how overly broad child neglect laws can fail families.

These statutes are being revisited as scholars , psychologists and journalists are increasingly finding fault with “helicopter parenting,” or overprotective parenting that limits children’s independence and autonomy.
Yet cases like Parkinson’s suggest that when the boundaries of neglect are unclear, the law continues to give parents a powerful incentive to err on the side of constant supervision.
In 1974, Congress passed the Child Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act to promote child safety and improve how child welfare services are provided.
The law provides federal funding to states to improve child protective services systems. It also requires states to have procedures for reporting instances of child abuse and neglect.
To obtain federal funding, states must comply with certain investigative procedures and reporting guidelines.
However, states enact their own laws on child abuse and neglect, each of which includes its own definitions and procedures, such as determining who must report suspected abuse or neglect.

In an effort to ensure instances of true neglect don’t fall through the cracks, state laws typically use vague language. Tennessee, for example, describes a neglected child as “under unlawful or improper care,” while Mississippi law categorizes a child as neglected if they are without “proper care, custody, supervision, or support.”

This is how a child whose mom has determined he’s mature enough to collect goose feathers on his own ends up being drawn into the system: An agency could argue that she wasn’t properly supervising him.
Other investigations of mothers for child neglect under similar circumstances have regularly cropped up over the past 20 years.

In 2013, an Illinois mother named Natasha Felix let her 11-, 9- and 5-year-old children play in the park adjacent to their home. Even though she could see them from the window, the state determined she met the definition of neglect due to inadequate supervision, a finding that was later reversed .

In 2014, a South Carolina mother , Debra Harrell, was working at a McDonald’s while her daughter was on summer vacation. During her shift, she allowed her 9-year-old daughter to play at a park about a mile away, giving her a cellphone in case she needed to get in touch. Harrell was arrested for felony child neglect, spent 17 days in jail and temporarily lost custody of her daughter.

A Georgia mother , Brittany Patterson, was investigated in 2024 because her 10-year-old son had taken a walk to a scenic mountain hamlet called Mineral Bluff, which was about a mile from his home. A woman saw him walking on the road and called the police. Law enforcement arrested the mother for reckless conduct. The charges were ultimately dismissed in 2025 .
Laws may encourage parents to be overprotective, but parenting research is recommending the opposite.

A 2020 study found that kids set free to roam on their own feel more confident navigating new places in adulthood . And other research has found that permissive parenting styles – the kind that can give kids opportunities to take risks, whether it’s climbing a tall structure on the playground or exploring the woods behind their house – help kids learn how to tolerate failure, distress and uncertainty , and ultimately develop into more competent adults .

That may explain why, in 2018, Utah amended its neglect statute to permit children to engage in independent activities like walking to school or playing outside, becoming the first state to do so. Since then, 12 states have amended neglect statutes to recognize childhood independence, including Georgia. After media coverage of Patterson’s case, Georgia lawmakers revised the legal definition of neglect to allow children of sufficient maturity and ability to engage in independent activities, such as playing outdoors or running errands to a convenience store. The definition further added that neglect should involve blatant disregard of parental responsibilities resulting in a real, significant and imminent risk of harm to the child.
Yet despite these efforts, parents continue to be punished for the decisions they’ve made when no harm was inflicted on the child.

A finding of neglect carries serious consequences. It can impact a parent’s future employment and can result in a child’s removal from the home. Concurrent criminal charges can carry penalties of imprisonment, fines and other conditions like attending parenting classes and mandated compliance with child protective services directives. Since mothers are more likely to be the primary caregiver , they face increased exposure and scrutiny under these laws.

The Virginia General Assembly also amended its child neglect definition in 2023 to clarify that children could engage in independent activities without adult supervision, like playing outdoors or traveling to nearby locations on foot or bicycle. It stipulated that activities simply needed to be age-appropriate and the child would not be endangered, but it didn’t define a minimum age for when children could be unsupervised.
In other words, the Legislature left it to parents to determine when their child would be mature enough to participate in unsupervised activities.
So how did Karyann Parkinson, who had no history of abuse or neglect, still get caught up in the system?

In the police report, the officer noted that the 5-year-old was walking unattended about a half-mile from his home, in close proximity to a pond. The officer also added that Parkinson “demonstrated no remorse” and that she believed her son was mature enough to walk there and back for the feathers.

Parkinson has argued that she decided to allow her son to collect feathers on his own to instill confidence in him, not to put him at risk. Her son had been placed in swimming lessons to ensure he would be safe around bodies of water.

Police officers, social workers and prosecutors all share a fear of overlooking abuse or harm. And to be sure, this has also happened: In 2025, a 32-year-old Connecticut man set fire to a home where he was allegedly being held captive for over two decades . Ensuing reporting found that child protection authorities had failed to identify and stop the alleged abuse in the years prior, despite repeated concerns raised by teachers and schoolmates.

When serious cases like this one come to light, the resulting media scrutiny can expose agencies to public criticism and cost state workers their jobs . This scrutiny can create incentives for law enforcement and child welfare agencies to investigate cases thoroughly.
At the same time, it can also foster a culture of overreaction.

A commonsense approach to child protection balances safety with knowledge of the specific child and parents involved. And I don’t think it’s in a state’s interest to have frivolous cases consume limited resources, particularly given the high turnover and heavy workloads in child protective services.

Jennifer L. Brinkley does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

articles.title: The science and politics behind the panic over ultraprocessed foods
articles.author:
<name>Garrett M. Broad, Professor of Communication Studies, Rowan University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/garrett-m-broad-231036"/>
paras: Ultraprocessed foods have a terrible reputation.

Studies have linked them with multiple chronic diseases . Journalists and health influencers characterize them as poison . Some public health experts call for a global halt to producing and consuming them.

But the debate around ultraprocessed foods is not nearly as settled as it may seem. As a researcher who studies social movements for healthy and sustainable food, I have been documenting the history of processed foods and examining debates around the science and politics of ultraprocessing .
In basic terms, ultraprocessed foods are mass-produced, industrial formulations that use ingredients not typically found in a home kitchen, and that generally contain little to no intact whole foods.

Yet the very definition of ultraprocessed is highly contested . While a growing number of advocates say that ultraprocessing is dangerous to public health, skeptics counter that the fervor around the topic has become a moral panic, and insist that some ultraprocessed foods can be part of a healthy diet.

People have been processing food – that is, transforming crops and animals into food ingredients and products – for all of human history. Cooking, which historians generally consider the first form of food processing , goes back as far as 2 million years. In the millennia and centuries that followed, people developed and refined other traditional food processing methods, including grinding, baking, fermenting, drying and pressing.

New types of food processing were created during the industrial age, beginning in the mid-18th century. Canning, pasteurization and refrigeration were among the major innovations that reshaped not only how people eat but society as a whole .

Before that time, nearly all food was local food – that is, produced within a few dozen miles – and people consumed fresh foods quickly to avoid spoilage. Food processing promised to improve food safety, shelf life, quality, convenience, taste and healthfulness. The world became more urbanized as regional and international supply chains developed. Geographically dispersed farmers were connected to retailers and consumers across the newly modern food system .

From the mid-20th into the 21st century, food manufacturers added a host of complex technological innovations to the food processing playbook. Their efforts made processed foods more standardized for the mass market and more convenient for consumers. But public health experts warned that processed junk foods were packed with salt, sugar and saturated fat – problematic nutrients linked to obesity, diabetes and other diet-related diseases.

By the mid-2000s, some healthy food advocates began to argue that the nature and extent of food processing, rather than the presence of specific problematic nutrients , explained diet-related chronic disease. The journalist Michael Pollan famously implored his audience to avoid “ edible food-like substances .” Instead, he advised: “Eat food. Not too much. Mostly plants.”

Brazilian epidemiologist Carlos Monteiro coined the term “ultraprocessing” in 2009 as part of his work on what he and colleagues called the NOVA classification . The NOVA framework establishes a four-category system that characterizes a food based on its level of processing.

NOVA Category 1 includes unprocessed or minimally processed plant or animal foods that are close to their natural state and contain no additives. Category 2 refers to processed culinary ingredients – that is, products derived from Category 1 via pressing, grinding or similar techniques. Category 3 describes processed foods made by combining Category 1 and Category 2 using traditional methods, such as baking, boiling or canning.

NOVA Category 4 foods are ultraprocessed foods, often described as industrially manufactured food products that can’t be made at home. Examples of ultraprocessing include separating whole foods into substances, chemically formulating foods or using cosmetic additives such as food dyes.

According to the framework, corporations design ultraprocessed foods to be convenient, hyperpalatable and highly profitable . They are packaged attractively, marketed intensively and intended to displace other food groups.

Today, ultraprocessed foods make up an increasingly large share of global diets . They account for more than 50% of total calories in the United States , with many low- and-middle income nations not far behind.
Since the NOVA framework emerged, researchers have tried to test whether food processing can explain how certain foods affect people’s health.

The vast majority of this work has explored correlations between consuming ultraprocessed foods and developing health problems. One consistent result stands out: People who consume more ultraprocessed foods are at higher risk for multiple chronic diseases and early death.

However, even that conclusion is more complex than it appears. It turns out that certain categories of ultraprocessed foods – such as sweetened beverages like sodas and processed meats like deli meats – are consistently associated with negative health outcomes including heart disease and stroke. But other ultraprocessed products – breads, cold cereals, yogurt and even savory snacks – have actually been correlated with lower rates of these health problems.
Still other ultraprocessed foods – including sauces, condiments and ready-to-heat dishes like frozen dinners – show no consistent links to people’s health one way or the other.

Only a handful of clinical trials that can actually show cause and effect have explored ultraprocessed foods’ effects on health . One prominent study did find that participants who ate a diet of ultraprocessed foods for two weeks consumed more calories and gained more weight than participants who followed a minimally processed diet, but other experiments have found no clear effect . What’s more, these studies generally last just a few weeks – far too short a time frame to draw conclusions about long-term health impacts.

Some food science researchers are unsurprised by these mixed findings, arguing that the definition of “ultraprocessed” is ambiguous and frequently subjective . For example, a cake prepared by a home baker would be considered a NOVA Category 3 “processed food.” But if that same cake were industrially manufactured using a commercial preservative, then packaged and sold at a grocery store, it would become a NOVA Category 4 “ultraprocessed food” – even if the two cakes were nutritionally identical.

Fundamentally, many nutrition scientists remain unconvinced that processing alone can explain why certain foods are associated with poor health. Instead, they emphasize that unhealthy ultraprocessed foods frequently have poor nutritional profiles and other qualities that make them easy to overeat. And they argue that making ultraprocessed foods healthier , not getting rid of them entirely, can improve public health.

Vilifying ultraprocessed foods may have harms, they suggest, like creating unnecessary fear and promoting disordered eating . It can also stigmatize eco-friendly, plant-based meats or ultraprocessed products such as baby formula that are designed for clinical nutrition .
The wholesale rejection of ultraprocessed foods could also make life more difficult for families who rely on the convenience and affordability the products offer.

On the other hand, many food policy and public health researchers maintain that the common definition of ultraprocessed is clear enough , especially if exceptions are made for healthy ultraprocessed foods. They also note that many supporters of ultraprocessed foods have ties to the food industry . They insist that the existing evidence is strong enough to take immediate policy action , including making changes to how ultraprocessed foods are produced, purchased and marketed.
Regulating ultraprocessed foods wouldn’t just benefit public health , advocates argue. It could also help rein in harms to food culture, business and the environment .

In this sense, ultraprocessed foods are a symptom of a bigger problem: an unsustainable industrial food system that is dominated by a handful of corporations. That argument, of course, is plenty contested too .

Ultimately, researchers and advocates from all sides of the debate mostly agree that the modern food environment needs to be made healthier. The key point of disagreement, however, is whether policymaking and dietary guidance should directly address ultraprocessing or stick to a more traditional focus on nutrients instead.

Garrett M. Broad is a board member with the non-profit Plant Based Foods Institute and an Advisory Board member with the non-profit New Jersey Food Democracy Collaborative, both on a non-remunerated basis. He has received research funding from the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA), National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), South Jersey Institute of Population Health, and Animal Charity Evaluators.

articles.title: Why and how US and Canadian energy markets are so deeply intertwined
articles.author:
<name>Stefano Tijerina, Senior Lecturer of Management, University of Maine</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/stefano-tijerina-1286882"/>
paras: The 50% tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump’s administration on imports from Canada in July 2026, and the reciprocal 50% tariffs imposed by Prime Minister Mark Carney’s administration on imports to Canada from the U.S. a month later, do not include oil and natural gas. Electricity and some petroleum products were also left out, although they remain subject to a 10% tariff imposed in 2025.

That’s because the two countries’ energy systems and markets are so intertwined that tariffs would devastate both economies. Canada is the biggest supplier of foreign petroleum to the United States, supplying half of all its petroleum imports . It is also the only direct foreign supplier of electricity to the U.S., with 34 major transmission points moving electricity from Canada south across the border.
In truth, Canada could shut down those power links and leave thousands of Americans in the dark , as Ontario provincial Premier Doug Ford threatened in August 2026.

But researchers like me , who study the historical links that have shaped Canadian and U.S. business relations, know that over the past 50 years Canada has expanded its energy production with one specific goal: serving U.S. consumption. In 2024, 84% of Canadian oil production and 76% of Canadian electricity production were exported to the U.S. Without American buyers, there is no real energy market in Canada.

Since the second half of the 19th century, energy generated on both sides of the border – and across them – has connected the two nations. The Great Lakes Basin was the hydraulic center of energy interconnectivity, as both nations shared the energy generated by Niagara Falls and the St. Lawrence River .

During the early stages of World War II, even before the U.S. entered the fight, Canada and the U.S. started to integrate their energy systems. That work was part of joint security efforts to protect North America through the integration of defense manufacturing production systems.

The Ogdensburg Declaration of 1940 and the 1941 Hyde Park Declaration consolidated and formalized the strategic economic and military cooperation between the two countries and set the foundations for future collaboration.
After the war, Canadian and U.S. businesses liked the idea of sharing production and manufacturing operations, even beyond war-related work.

Nevertheless, manufacturing on both sides of the border went back to prewar ways of producing things domestically. Nationalist voices opposed the idea of further integrating the Canadian and U.S. economies.

Less than two decades after the war ended, though, the two nations signed the Auto Pact of 1965 , which eliminated tariffs on cars, trucks and automotive parts. Canadian parts manufacturers could compete directly with those based in the U.S., all to serve U.S. automakers.
This initial experiment in free trade revealed to businesses on both sides of the border that supply chain integration could benefit other production and service industries.

By 1989, the two countries had signed a full-scale free trade agreement that removed tariffs for goods crossing the border in either direction. That opened the door for more closely integrating their energy markets too.

In 1992, a U.S. federal law changed a wide swath of regulations over the country’s energy markets. Some of the provisions allowed Canadian companies to sell excess energy to the U.S., and two years later the North American Free Trade Agreement brought Mexico into the relationship too.
NAFTA integrated the production, processing and distribution of thousands of goods and services across all three countries.

But it was the interconnection of energy infrastructure that turned the Canadian and U.S. economies into one single energy market. Today, four major U.S. electrical grids depend on imported power from Canada: those serving the six New England states , New York state , 15 states across the Midwest and the South , and California .

Moreover, there are more than 40 natural gas and petroleum liquids pipelines connecting Canada with the United States. And although energy products move back and forth across the border, the U.S. has an energy trade deficit with Canada. Much of the U.S. economy runs on Canadian energy, and much of Canada’s energy production is sold to the U.S.
The current reality on the ground shows an integrated energy system between the two nations: something very difficult and costly to untangle, and a process that would take decades to reengineer.
Today, those links form the basis for very tight integration between the two countries’ business and industrial marketplaces.
For example, Maine, where I live and work, gets close to 30% of its electricity from Canada.
The state’s northern electrical grid is run by the New Brunswick Power Corp. , owned by the province of New Brunswick, which serves close to 60,000 Mainers.

Today, Maine’s electric grid is owned mostly by foreign interests, including ENMAX, the municipally owned utilities corporation of Calgary, Alberta , and the owner of Versant Power, which serves 16% of Maine’s market. And 80% is served by Central Maine Power, which is owned by Iberdrola from Spain.

Canadian energy reaches deeper into the U.S., too. In 2025, Hydro-Quebec, a company that generates electricity from dams across the province of Quebec , secured a deal with local regulators to use Maine as a corridor to supply clean energy to Massachusetts. Hydro-Quebec is owned by the government of the province of Quebec.
The bilateral integration of energy infrastructure over the past 30-plus years explains why this sector was exempt from the most recent tariffs.

articles.title: How candidates are (quietly) talking about climate change – 3 election strategies you’ll see across the US
articles.author:
<name>Geoffrey Henderson, Assistant Professor, School for Environment and Sustainability, University of Michigan</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/geoffrey-henderson-2762895"/>
paras: Amid wars, inflation, emerging risks from artificial intelligence and threats to democracy, Americans have a lot to be worried about these days. But polls show the majority of voters in 2026 are also concerned about climate change as temperatures and disaster risks rise.
So why are fewer candidates talking openly about climate change in their midterm election campaigns than just a few years ago ?
At the University of Michigan’s School for Environment and Sustainability, we study climate communication and are following how Democratic candidates are discussing climate change in their campaigns.

Democratic candidates seem to agree on one strategy: campaign centrally on affordability, emphasizing how ordinary people are struggling to afford to fill up their cars , pay their electric bills and insure their homes against hurricanes and wildfires. It’s part of a concerted effort to make the election a referendum on Republicans’ support for the Trump administration’s contributions to inflation, such as tariffs and the Iran war.

Fossil fuel industry interests have long sought to polarize the public over the phrase “climate change.” As one of us, Geoffrey Henderson, discusses in his new book , “Getting to Work on Climate Policy: The Strategy of Labor-Environmental Coalitions,” campaigns pitting economic concerns against environmental ones have made it harder to build support for policies meant to slow climate change.
When it comes to talking about climate change today, three distinct camps of Democratic candidates and officeholders reveal three different strategies.
The energy populists talk a lot about lowering energy prices for consumers but very little about either climate change or fossil fuels.

Many have been painting data centers , rather than fossil fuel producers, as villains. Candidates often use messages focused on how utilities and data centers are raising voters’ electric rates. They propose measures to lower these costs, like requiring data centers to bring their own energy sources onto the grid.

In North Carolina, former governor Roy Cooper, now running for U.S. Senate, emphasizes lowering energy and utility costs . Sherrod Brown of Ohio, campaigning to return to the Senate, argues that his opponent’s votes in favor of data centers have led to “ higher electric rates .”

Discussing energy affordability, without directly calling out the risks to the climate from burning fossil fuels or advocating for more renewable energy, aligns with the argument that climate change messages can alienate swing voters , who prioritize affordability.

If energy populists are elected, they could become silent backers of climate policies to reduce greenhouse gas emissions – both Brown and Cooper have a record of supporting renewable energy – or obstacles to climate policies.
Not all Democrats, even in battleground states, think climate change should fade into the background this election. However, few are as outspoken today as they were in the past.

In Massachusetts, Sen. Ed Markey’s website pledges that he will champion “ bold action to invest in clean energy ” if reelected in November. In Maine, Senate candidate Troy Jackson asserts that politicians should not pit working-class people against renewable energy, casting the climate-versus-affordability debate as a false choice.

Rhode Island’s Sheldon Whitehouse, one of the Senate’s most outspoken supporters of pro-climate policies, contends that candidates should link higher costs to climate change , such as increased home insurance costs due to hurricane risk. He also points to President Donald Trump’s blockade of the cheapest energy sources – namely, solar and wind power – which he attributes to fossil fuel industry influence.

If elected, these candidates’ messages suggest they will pursue policies that help reduce U.S. contributions to climate change. However, they may need to convince independent voters that their focus on climate change will not overshadow their attention to other challenges.

Another group of candidates wants to have it both ways. They call for actions that can respond to climate change and rapidly build out renewable energy, while also promising cheaper gasoline and more fossil fuel jobs. Scientists warn that more fossil fuel use cuts against global climate goals .

Unlike the other camps, this group does not identify villains in their narrative. These candidates are following the script from the Obama administration, whose “all of the above” energy strategy espoused continued fossil fuel use alongside policies to reduce planet-warming emissions.

In Iowa, U.S. Senate candidate Josh Turek hosted a roundtable in April 2026 on how climate-fueled extreme weather is raising insurance costs . But he has also focused on lowering the cost of gasoline and diesel . James Talarico, campaigning for the Senate in Texas, has similarly promised to fight climate change by boosting renewable energy while lowering costs by promoting all energy sources.

These candidates may be trying to signal their potential to support climate policies while respecting their states’ cultural connections to fossil fuels. Turek and Talarico are both running in states with abundant wind power .
Studies from the U.S. and Germany find that politicians usually underestimate public support for efforts to address climate change.
So how well do candidates’ platforms represent today’s voters?

Yale’s spring 2026 survey found that 49% of voters believe global warming should be a high priority for Congress and the president. But 70% of moderate or conservative Democrats share this view, alongside 84% of liberal Democrats. Even 1 in 3 liberal-to-moderate Republicans considers the climate a high priority.

Yet polling also suggests that other issues, such as the increasing cost of living, are even more important to many voters . This data suggests that pro-climate messages could appeal to swing voters most strongly if climate policies are seen as complementary to affordability.

Still, a recent survey shows that voters open to Democratic candidates are more likely to support a candidate who prioritizes climate change. Climate messaging may especially resonate with young voters. Over a third of those ages 18 to 29 in a recent Harvard Youth Poll considered climate change an urgent national crisis . Young Republicans are more supportive of addressing climate change than their older counterparts.

While many shifts in the way candidates talk about climate policy have little impact on people’s willingness to participate in collective efforts to address it, messages emphasizing cost savings durably increase support for renewable energy across party lines. Voters’ current concerns about inflation could make climate messages involving affordability especially effective in 2026, though the impact of these messages may vary from state to state .

These different approaches reflect the Democratic Party’s efforts to build a “big tent” that can attract voters with a wide range of views and priorities. Yet Democrats are generally coalescing around a message designed to appeal to working-class voters: that Trump and the Republicans are raising your cost of living.
November’s midterm elections will offer some insight into whether Democrats’ energy affordability message will resonate in the 2028 presidential election.
Geoffrey Henderson has worked on a project that received funding from the National Science Foundation.
Nathaniel Geiger has received funding from the National Science Foundation.

articles.title: Students take up to 88 standardized tests before high school, but more testing doesn’t improve learning
articles.author:
<name>Liza Bondurant, Associate Professor of Secondary Math Education, Mississippi State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/liza-bondurant-1515994"/>
paras: The public K-12 school system in the United States has become pervasively shaped by standardized testing.
I began teaching mathematics in 2005, four years after the federal law No Child Left Behind was enacted. This law expanded state testing and tied test results to school performance.
Most districts changed their curricula to focus more on the content and skills covered on state tests.
Many school districts increased their instructional weekly time for English and mathematics, with average increases of 47% for English and 37% for mathematics from 2001 to 2007.
To make room for additional time spent on these subjects, 44% of school districts cut time from other subjects or activities, such as the arts.
A 2026 study of 67 school districts across 38 states found that, before high school, students take a median of 57 state- and district-required assessments.
No Child Left Behind was replaced by another law, the Every Student Succeeds Act , in 2015.

Although the Every Student Succeeds Act aimed to reduce the role of testing in classrooms, standardized tests continue to shape what teachers teach, how they use instructional time and how schools define success.

All U.S. public schools are required to administer standardized tests in reading and math annually to students in grades three through eight and at least once in high school. These tests measure whether students are reading and understanding mathematics at, above or below the average, when compared to other students across the state.
Students’ scores on these tests can affect schools’ ratings and rankings, and can also determine whether states monitor or take over public school districts that are not performing well.

The exact number of tests students take each year before high school ranges from 35 to 88 tests. The study also found no relationship between the number of assessments students took and their proficiency or growth in English or mathematics.
The National Association of State Boards of Education also reports that some districts give students seven assessments per grade, with most tests administered one to three times a year.
Older research also documents the time teachers spend preparing students for state tests.

A 2016 survey found that 62% of K-12 public school teachers reported spending too much time preparing students for state-mandated tests. Teachers estimated spending an average of 14 out of 180 school days preparing students for these exams, whether it be reviewing the question formats students see on tests or teaching test-taking strategies.
In the same 2016 national survey, 29% of teachers reported spending more than a month preparing students in grades K-12 for state-mandated tests.
Teachers also feel the effects of spending so much time preparing students for standardized tests.
Research on teacher turnover has found that teachers’ dissatisfaction with standardized testing was a key reason they left the profession.
Other research from 2026 found that teachers who worried about job consequences tied to test results reported lower job satisfaction.
These numbers tell a larger story. The costs of standardized testing do not simply appear in the amount printed on contracts with testing companies.

They are also reflected in lesson plans, teachers’ workloads, classroom time, professional autonomy and the opportunities that disappear when preparing for a test becomes a central purpose of schooling.

A test can measure learning. But when some students take as many as 88 assessments before high school and teachers report spending weeks preparing students for state exams, it’s important to ask whether it’s the best use of their limited time.

I work in Mississippi, where many communities are rural and agriculture is a major industry. Recently, I lamented to a local farmer about the time and money spent on standardized testing. He offered a simple response: “You don’t get a pig to grow by measuring it more.” His words capture the question at the heart of this debate: Does more testing help students learn, or does it take time away from learning?

articles.title: Sunday Movie: Service-Led Planning in California Rail
articles.author: Mike Orr
paras: In 2004 California released an excellent service-led plan to expand its state rail network, both the high-speed rail projects and other corridors and a few BRT connectors. This video by nandert goes in-depth on why service-led planning is an important paradigm all agencies should use (5:33), the benefits of California’s plan, and how the governing boards would need major structural changes and reforming their priorities to actually make it happen this well.

He defines service-led planning as “Start by determining where the transit demand and need is, and tailor the plan to meet that demand.” In other words, determining how much of what kind of service each corridor needs. Then draw up cost estimates for the resulting lines to operators (agencies). The California plan specifies the rail/bus mode and frequency, but you could also leave the mode for a later step before assigning them to agencies, as Jarrett Walker does.

The difference between this and most transit planning is, corridors are chosen to meet the bulk of mobility/trip needs, without certain city/county jurisdictions having undue influence to override these for demands that contradict them. It also puts frequency first in the spec rather than leaving is as an afterthought, so the public can see what minimum frequency the entire network or each project will have so that they can see what their experience will be like.

articles.title: Pikes/Pines | Mega mammoths and giant manroots: the natural history behind your Hilloween pumpkin
articles.author: Brendan McGarry
paras: Your’s truly sitting on a Cucurbita maxima (Image: Brendan McGarry)

Nothing says autumn like pumpkins. Jack-o-lanterns. Pumpkin pie. Pumpkin spiced lattes. Pumpkin Beer. Fields of pumpkins (and their three sisters cohort, corn, as a maze). Pumpkins are such an integral part of American culture that we don’t really have to think of them, they are just there every fall, taken for granted and left unexamined despite littering porches across Capitol Hill and the country between now and Thanksgiving.
Turns out they are wonders of human/plant mutualism, formed by cultural and ecological change.

These fruits that we broadly call squashes are deeply of the places we call the Americas today. Archeological evidence suggests that people living in present day Mexico and Central America were using pumpkins as a staple crop over 10,000 years ago — so long ago that it feels almost foolish calling them an “American” fruit. Before people started breeding them into their present, and varied, forms, we likely have large herbivores like Mastodons and Mammoths to thank for the widespread range of wild pumpkins that indigenous people came to grow.

Research suggests that the bitter seeds of the wild pumpkins deterred most animal herbivory, except large herbivores that were less sensitive and ate them whole, dispersing the seeds mixed in a pile of soon to be compost. An enjoyable research paper from 2015 , theorizes that when these megafauna disappeared, because of humans, pumpkins found a new way to be successful through human mutualism. Modern wild elephants in Africa today demonstrate the same sort of dispersal with wild squashes that are largely ignored by other animals.

The pumpkins of old bore only superficial resemblance (at least in fruit), to the pumpkins of today. Thousands of years of genetic fiddling by humans have given us the tasty, (nearly) entirely edible fruits. Pumpkins are members of the Cucurbitaceae family, which is a nearly global group of plants with around 1000 species, including other squashes, melons, and cucumbers. All of the plants we call pumpkins are in the new world genus Cucurbita, of which several species have been domesticated. According to Logan Kistler, author of the paper mentioned above paper above and Curator of Archaeobotany and Archaeogenomics at the Smithsonian, Cucurbita species may have been domesticated at least six times, in as many places. Debate still flies about the way these plants are classified and their exact origins, understandable for plants that readily hybridize, transport well, and are genetically complex.

We broadly know the origins of modern pumpkins. From Cucurbita pepo , we have the classic fruit of pumpkin patches and jack-o-lanterns, along with the classic winter squashes, zucchinis, and other summer squashes. Less often called a pumpkin, but of close relation and equal agricultural importance today, is Cucurbita moschata , commonly called crookneck squashes, from which we have many modern crops like Butternut Squash and Calabaza, but most notably the variety that fills nearly pumpkin pie filling you buy on the shelf, the Dickinson pumpkin. And of course there is Cucurbita maxima, which has spawned the monstrously huge pumpkins seen at state fairs and growing competitions, (the largest on record was grown this year, weighing in at 2,856.8 lbs).
All pumpkins are squashes but not all squashes are considered pumpkins. Which are these? (Image: Brendan McGarry)

A good many of us have heard of the three sisters, corn, beans, and squash and their agricultural significance in many indigenous cultures across North America. We wouldn’t have the pumpkins of today without thousands of years of relationship, without people who were stewards of and had a reciprocal relationship with the plants. We also wouldn’t have the specific varieties we regularly see today without things like capitalism and industrial scale agriculture. When you hold a pumpkin in your hands, they have heft to them, and that heft is partly born of the complexity of their existence in our modern day.

The tradition of carving pumpkins is one of those things that has morphed and changed with people and culture. The C. pepo that fill fields and adorn porches plain, or as Jack-o-lanterns (a term that sprung from the old name for marsh gases spontaneously combusting), has a shallow connection to the Gaelic holiday Samhain, the progenitor of Halloween. A tradition of carving and lighting turnips and other large root crops during Samhain was brought to America by immigrants from Ireland and other countries in the British Isles. However, with access to large, readily carvable pumpkins, the turnips were spurned and pumpkins adopted. What was once a way to connect with wayward spirits or ward off the Aos Sí of the Otherworld during a time of thin boundaries between our worlds is now mostly just an extension of late state capitalism a la Spirit Halloween.

There’s a temptation to leave the idea that pumpkins were important indigenous crops in the Americas equally unexamined. While an indisputable fact, it doesn’t invite us to consider the complexity of the peoples and the places that the “Americas” represents. In this part of the world the first people had no pumpkins, in fact no squash, and a very different relationship with tending plants born of climate, ecology, and the resulting cultures they influenced. Many important plants (are and) were certainly tended, but they were wild plants, visited at pivotal times of year but mostly left to their own devices — an entirely different (but no less complex) form of land management.

However, there is a sole member of the Cucurbitaceae family native to Washington, Capitol Hill included. Coastal Manroot, or Marah oregana is a wild cucumber that sprawls over open areas across lowland western Washington. While the plant’s leaves and fruit have traditional uses throughout its range, it is also highly toxic, full of those bitter pest deterrents, cucurbitacins that likely had a role in prehuman pumpkin dispersal by mammoths and mastodons. The name “manroot” comes from the enormous tuber, which can truly become human-sized and weigh two hundred pounds. I’ve not seen Coastal Manroot on the Hill, but there are several iNaturalist records of it and I am sure some of the less manicured corners may host the plant. Few would invite it into their yards because they are extremely vigorous and rapidly cover anything within reach, even Himalayan Blackberry.

If you had any doubt that pumpkins have deep stories, hopefully now you see how wonderfully interesting these commonplace plants are. And even if the botanist in me wants to tell you that their fruits are technically a berry, I can also let you enjoy them for what they are to you. Maybe you just like pumpkin spice (which really isn’t pumpkin flavored at all) or god forbid, pumpkin beer and that’s ok. As long as we attempt to appreciate where these things come from (those spices though, they are not American whatsoever, well except for Allspice). As Mary Oliver said, “attention is the beginning of devotion,” and I couldn’t agree more. I see you, pumpkins.

articles.title: Op-Ed: Bremerton Should Fully Pedestrianize Quincy Square
articles.author: Travis Merrigan
paras: The City of Bremerton is debating how to use the newly completed, $4 million Quincy Square, located at the heart of downtown. As with Seattle’s Pike Place Market, Bremerton Public Works proposed closing the ‘Q Square’ about half the days of the year. At a Sept 3rd City Council meeting, councilors were split 3-to-3 between supporting the 182-day closure and seeking more car-access days. It’s just the latest debate in an on-going tug of war as the city tries to carve out safe multimodal spaces from Bremerton’s thoroughly car-dominated streets and neighborhoods.

Completed in 2025, Quincy Square is a half-block of 4th Street in the heart of downtown. It features a permanent stage, seating and tables, and interactive music installations honoring the late, great music impresario Quincy Jones, who spent his middle school years in Bremerton, before moving to Seattle.

Q Square was designed as a hybrid street, transforming via mid-block, removable bollards between pedestrian-oriented plaza and a one-way street with 14 parking spots. The debate this fall at Bremerton City Council is about how many days the plaza should be open to cars.

The Public Works plan attempts to split the baby, via middle-of-the-road Resolution No. 3417. The resolution would change Bremerton city code to create ‘pedestrian mall’, under a little used Washington state law from the 1960s. On September 3, City Council voted 5-1 to create a pedestrian mall, but a major rift formed over whether Q Square should be primarily a pedestrian street closed to cars or just a regular street which closes sometimes for events.

Public Works’ initial proposal offered a vision of Quincy Square offering economic, safety and social benefits of a predictable schedule and community gathering space. It also cited the costs of the current, on-again off-again street closures, including resource drain and overtime required to replace signage and bollards at odd hours. The administration’s plan also cited confused drivers, forced into awkward u-turns on a street that might be open the day before.

Public Works is seeking guidance on a separate, administrative decision, to set the calendar which designates which days Q Square is open to traffic. The initial proposal was for about 182 days closed, concentrated in the summer and between Thanksgiving and New Years, with the plaza open to traffic the other 183 days.

During its September 3rd deliberations, Council was split 3-3 (with one councilmember absent) between closing Q Square to cars for at least 182-days per year, and three councilors who sought more car-access days.

Opponents of more pedestrianization of Q Square have understandable and sincere concerns about the downsides of closing the street. People who park or drive on the street are being asked to shoulder a disproportionate burden of an amenity that benefits the entire city.
Those opposing more pedestrianization of Q Square have three primary complaints:

Every multimodal project that restricts automobile access faces backlash from those who would otherwise have unfettered usage of a given space. Q Square is home to four dozen businesses, including a theater, corner store, skate shop and over 30 professional offices in a mid-rise tower. For those people, it’s more convenient to get dropped off right in front of the door than walk from a parking garage or street parking 200 feet away.

And opponents argue that, with the exception of City-sponsored events, the Square is little-used. That too few people - or the wrong kinds of people (e.g., unhoused) - hang out in the Square to justify the loss of parking and car traffic. This echoes a common criticism of ‘empty’ bike lanes; if somebody isn’t constantly in them, the space should be available for cars.

Bremerton must decide if the creation of a central, community gathering space is worth forcing inconvenience on a few dozen drivers every day. This half block of 4th St is probably downtown’s lowest-traffic street, and the 14 parking stalls are just 0.2% of downtown’s 6,300 public parking spaces. And many city amenities - parks, free street parking, park benches, and schools - sit empty most hours of the year. These amenities are valuable because they are available when needed. Nobody tears down a church because it’s empty on a Tuesday afternoon.

The status quo of random 4th Street closures leads to confused motorists making awkward half-block u-turns on a street not fit for purpose. The street could be reconfigured as a u-shaped drop-off site for cars and shuttle buses, with short-term, off-hour parking for deliveries. Resolution 3417 allows acquisition of right of way, and the affected hotel would likely welcome an improvement to the chaotic turn-arounds.

Leaving Q Square closed for long blocks of time allows drivers and businesses to adjust and find new hacks to efficiently navigate and do commerce downtown. Meanwhile, designating Q Square for pedestrians will, over time, attract more people downtown, and delight visitors who stumble across the open space.

Great cities have great plazas. Plazas are where poems are written, friends meet for lunch and kids first learn to ride bikes. The $4 million Quincy Square is brand new and, if left open for people to gather, will become the beating heart of thriving downtown Bremerton. Q Square will help downtown recover from the suburban flight of the 80s and 90s which pulled commerce out of the city, off to distant strip malls outside the city.

In modern-day Bremerton, virtually every inch of downtown street is maximized for vehicles. Among downtown’s 6,300 public parking spots are four, city-owned, multistory parking garages. Most downtown streets host two-way traffic plus dual-side on-street parking. Pedestrians are shunted aside onto narrow sidewalks, with few benches to sit on or places to linger. Street eateries that granted street life to downtown during the pandemic are nearly all swept away, to make room for street parking. The nearest playground swing is 0.75 miles away.

Revitalization of downtown requires people to get out of their cars, window shop and spend money in downtown businesses. A lovely, welcoming square that encourages people to linger will benefit many businesses downtown, even if the lost parking affects some more than others.

Bremerton could take action to reduce the hyperlocal problems caused by vehicle restrictions. Additional short-term and ADA parking could be created very near Q Square. The City could designate the four Pacific Avenue parking stalls nearest Q Square as ADA and place 2-hour parking limits on the bottom two floors of its 4th and Washington parking garage. Also, an improved turn-around and drop-off spot could be created in collaboration with the hotel immediately east of the half-block vehicle barriers.

More people would use Q Square if the city offered very low-cost rental of the space for bike polo matches, band rehearsals and mass outdoor Dungeons and Dragons tournaments (Bremerton’s nerd game is strong). The burden of filling the square need not fall on the City funding big events.

Opponents of closing Q Square predict terrible outcomes. But outcomes will probably be less dire than they predict, especially if Bremerton makes adjustments. Besides, unexpected upsides are just as likely as miserable downsides. Cities have always thrived because of spontaneous interaction in public places, which sparks ideas, creates new commerce and builds community. Q Square is unique in all of Bremerton, but common across the world: a safe, inviting, central plaza where people go just because, and where interesting and unexpected things can happen.
Great cities have great plazas. Quincy Square is Bremerton’s once-in-a-generation shot to create Bremerton’s first great plaza. Let’s not throw away our shot.
The Bremerton City Council will debate the Mayor’s proposal at an upcoming council meeting this fall.

articles.title: Amazon’s new Bee AI devices have a bystander problem, says former AWS security engineer
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Amazon’s new Bee AI devices ask the wrong person for consent, according to a privacy and security veteran who previously worked as a senior principal security engineer at Amazon Web Services.
In a LinkedIn article , Jeff Williams writes that Bee’s consent safeguards are aimed at the wearer, while the people being recorded have no practical way to say no.

Amazon unveiled the devices Thursday , the first new Bee hardware since it acquired the San Francisco startup last year. The $74.99 Bee Frontier goes on the wrist or clips to clothing, and the $99.99 Bee Eclipse snaps onto the back of a phone.
Both turn conversations into summaries and to-do lists, with connections to Amazon.com and Alexa+ for paid subscribers.
How Bee handles consent: Amazon says users are prompted to get permission from call participants each time they start a recording, and the devices show an indicator light while in use.

The problem, Williams says, is that neither one reliably tells the other people in a conversation that they’re being recorded. He writes that the prompt appears only on the wearer’s phone, and nothing enforces it.
“A prompt instructing the user to obtain permission is a liability allocation,” he wrote, arguing that Amazon is shifting responsibility for obtaining consent onto the wearer.
The light is easy to hide under a sleeve or in a pocket, he notes, and a device on the wrist or phone sits outside the frame on a video call.

Williams points to Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses as an example. In September, the data protection authority in Hamburg , Germany, found the glasses’ recording light hard to see outdoors and concluded that a recording indicator alone doesn’t establish informed consent under Europe’s GDPR.
In the U.S., about a dozen states, including Washington state and California, generally require consent from everyone before a private conversation can be recorded.

Whose data is protected: Williams gives Amazon credit for Bee Private Compute, which processes audio in an isolated, encrypted environment built on AWS Nitro and then deletes it. Amazon says only the customer can access the resulting data, not Amazon or Bee.

But that protects the wearer. The words of the people around the wearer still end up in transcripts and summaries they can’t see or remove. Amazon says those speakers aren’t identified by name unless they complete a voice training exercise with the device’s owner.
Williams notes that Amazon has changed comparable privacy commitments before, such as ending the “Do Not Send Voice Recordings” option on some Echo devices last year.

Williams also advises companies to keep the devices out of client meetings and privileged discussions, since the transcripts end up in an employee’s personal account, where the company can’t see or manage them.

A proposed fix: Williams says Bee should leave other people’s voices out of transcripts by default, unless they’ve enrolled their voices and agreed to be recorded. Before the acquisition, Bee indicated plans to record only the voices of people who had verbally consented, according to TechCrunch .
“I know first-hand that Amazon has the engineering talent to ship it,” he wrote.
Amazon’s response: The company didn’t comment directly on the critique but pointed to safeguards built into the devices.

One is an automatic shutoff: the devices turn off if they don’t detect the owner’s voice for 5, 15, 30 or 60 minutes, depending on the user’s setting. Amazon says that reinforces that Bee is “a personal AI assistant, not a device designed to passively pick up audio throughout the day.”

The company says it educates customers about responsible use in the Bee app, and that Eclipse will send push notifications encouraging users to let people around them know they’re using Bee and to ask for permission.

Williams, now chief information security officer at Sigma360, worked at AWS from 2023 to 2025 and spent more than 12 years at Microsoft before that, including as a privacy officer for its services business. Read his full article on LinkedIn. Read his full article on LinkedIn.
