articles.title: How ICE Continues to Wield Washington's Own Data
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: In the wake of accelerated immigration enforcement by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) across the country this summer and into fall, new data shows that Washington state driver data is still being used to enable and assist in these arrests.

The update comes from the University of Washington Center of Human Rights (UWCHR), which published an initial report at the beginning of the year showing how Washington state driver data was being accessed to assist in federal immigration enforcement. Now, nine months later, UWCHR has data showing this practice has continued unabated. Researchers have confirmed 356 arrest incidents between August 1, 2025 and October 13, 2026 that have resulted from federal agents receiving Washington State Department of Licensing (DOL) driver data through the interstate querying system Nlets.

“We know that 356 is likely only a small fraction of the total cases that are happening,” said UWCHR Director Angelina Godoy at a press conference on Tuesday. “Those are just the ones where we were able to confirm it with smoking gun evidence connecting a given plate search to a known immigration arrest.”
ICE continues to access this DOL data in spite of the 2019 Keep Washington Working Act and government officials being aware of this data access pathway since at least 2018, according to the report.

Federal agents’ general operating procedure is to travel to target-rich environments where they think they might find immigrants. They ask the state for data about certain license plates via Nlets, run the registered owner names they are given via Nlets through their own databases, and then decide whether to make an arrest.

Nilu Jenks, a candidate for the District 5 seat of the Seattle City Council, wants to add the Seattle Police Department’s use of Nlets to the Office of the Inspector General’s annual surveillance review while also calling for action from the state legislature and Governor Bob Ferguson.

“In District 5, ‘target rich’ is a polite way of saying racial profiling,” said Jenks. “It means agents deciding who looks deportable by the color of their skin and the work truck they drive: the roofer outside a hardware store on Aurora, the landscaping crew in Maple Leaf, the dad dropping his kids at school in Lake City. When a license plate becomes a name and home address in moments, every trip is a risk. Nobody should have to wonder whether it's safe to drive because of how they look, and no state database should help put a target on their backs.”
Godoy underlined that Washington state hasn’t been doing enough to address the increasing levels of violence and fear experienced by immigrant residents.

“This is a time of extraordinary pain and difficulty for immigrant communities in Washington and around our country, not only because we are experiencing unprecedented levels of immigration enforcement here in the region and around the country, but also because we're experiencing the use of increasingly violent tactics, which appear to involve overt racial profiling, often warrantless arrests, which challenge the Constitution,” Godoy said. “Multiple courts around the nation have found these practices to be unconstitutional, in fact, but here in Washington, this has been greeted thus far with relative silence, which I believe contributes to the invisibilization and isolation of immigrant communities in our midst.”

Immigration enforcement has quietly increased across the country this summer, with ICE eschewing the more dramatic “surges” it conducted earlier in the year in Minneapolis, Chicago, and other cities. Washington state has been no exception to this swell, and Godoy said she expects to see the numbers continue to rise over time.
The Seattle Times reported that 74% of ICE arrests in Washington in June and July did not involve people with criminal convictions or pending charges.

Guillermo Rivera from Eastside for All, an equity advocacy organization, spoke about the detentions being observed on the Eastside at the press conference. “Most of these cases happen when people were driving, or close to their vehicles, or inside their vehicles, and this is not only happening in East King County, this is happening all around the state,” Rivera said. “The people are being detained when they are driving. People, we are afraid now to go into our cars, that they can stop us at any time. We're afraid to go to the supermarket, to take the kids to the doctor, to take our children to school.”

The UWHRC report described a common new technique being seen in ICE detentions known as “jump outs.” “Jump outs” involve multiple unmarked vehicles, sometimes lacking license plates, surrounding a target who is driving. Unidentified officers then jump out of their cars and violently detain their target. Officers often already know the name of the person they are detaining due to the state driver data they have accessed.
The “jump out” has become one of ICE’s key enforcement strategies since President Donald Trump began his second term.

19 of 22 shootings by immigration agents in Trump’s second term have taken place during these ICE traffic stops, an analysis this summer found, with the UWHRC identifying at least two additional ICE shootings during traffic stops since then.

The increasing brutality of immigration enforcement is also typified by two recent investments by ICE: up to $2 million on robot dogs and up to $20 million on gloves that deliver painful electric shocks.

Meanwhile, local lawmakers still don’t know if ICE is planning to buy the Northwest Detention Center in Tacoma, which could stymie state efforts to impose oversight on the facility. ICE’s current contract with the facility is set to expire on October 27.

The detention center has been receiving complaints about poor and dehumanizing conditions for years. Indeed, conditions there are so bad that Washington State Senator Yasmin Trudeau (D-Tacoma) refers to the facility as a concentration camp.

UW researchers found evidence that in Minnesota, driver data queries were also being used to obtain information about community observers of ICE activity, which shows how similar tactics can be used to both increase immigration detentions and to surveil U.S. citizens without a warrant.
The UWHRC also found evidence that this practice is happening right here in King County.

This past June, community member Tony Andrews saw a suspicious vehicle in a Fred Meyer parking lot in Bellevue. Andrews had attended a constitutional observer training through Indivisible Eastside, which allowed him to identify the vehicle as possibly belonging to ICE. Even though Andrews kept his distance, the suspicious vehicle circled tightly around Andrews’ car in the parking lot.

Andrews gave his vehicle information to the UW researchers who submitted a records request. The returned records showed that his license plate had been run through Nlets on the day and time that the incident with the suspicious vehicle took place.
“For me, this was just a violation of my privacy,” Andrews told The Urbanist . “For the immigrants, these violations are life-changing. For them, it can mean family separation.”
The UWHRC report detailed four different pathways by which ICE and other federal agents are able to get state driver data:
The report emphasized that all pathways must be addressed simultaneously; otherwise ICE will simply shift to a new means of accessing the data.
In Washington state, ICE had been accessing driver data via direct access to the state DMV databases as recently as last year , but for now, that pathway appears to be closed.

DOL sold its data to 14 companies last year, including at least three who held Department of Homeland Security (DHS) contracts in the near past. While these contracts with DOL forbid the data brokers from selling the data for immigration enforcement purposes, one of the companies, LexisNexis, has structured at least one past contract with ICE in such a way that LexisNexis would have no ability to see how ICE has been using the data. Therefore, it is impossible to be confident that ICE cannot use the data broker pathway to access Washington state driver data.
Direct agency sharing data with ICE is illegal under the Keep Washington Working Act, although that doesn’t mean it isn’t happening anyway.
However, the primary way ICE appears to be accessing DMV data in Washington state at this time is through the Nlets queries.

Governor Bob Ferguson has said that his office’s actions of canceling ICE and DHS’s access to Nlets has resulted in blocking 100,000 attempts to use Nlets to access state data. However, the UWHRC report found that from January 1, 2025 to May 31, 2026, DHS-affiliated agencies still searched the DOL database via Nlets 3,696,147 times, showing the gaping hole in the state’s data protections.

“What happens is that those arrest patrols, whether they're made of ICE, of the Border Patrol, of combined agencies, or of unknown masked men, simply log in under another agency's ORI, just like you might share your Netflix password with a family member,” Godoy said. “As a result, between January and June 2026, Washington DOL data itself shows that over one million searches were completed of Washington driver and vehicle data by agencies who are part of DHS.”
So far UWHRC has documented 38 unique ORIs, or passwords, affiliated with federal agencies prior to arrests by ICE and U.S. Customs and Border Patrol (CBP) in Washington state.

The report did find that New York State has been successful at cutting off the Nlets channel of information via robust legislation. In New York, federal agents are now only able to search out-of-state license plates via Nlets.

Pacific Rim Solidarity Network sent a statement to be read at the press conference instead of coming to speak due to fears of retaliation. They called for Ferguson to enable more transparency and accountability when it comes to DOL data sharing.

“Legislatures take time, and our communities need an answer now. We cannot wait until the next fall to have protections for Washington residents,” Rivera said. “We're asking the governor's office to act now. We're asking the governor to review how this information is being collected, how it's been shared, find any gaps or misuse, and use his authority to protect Washington residents.”

If Ferguson continues to choose not to close these documented gaps, the state legislature can act in January to make the Keep Washington Working Act more robust. Godoy emphasized that being even more explicit about the need for a court warrant in order to access state driver data wouldn’t be sufficient.

“The state has already incorporated specific requirements that Nlets comply with Keep Washington Working or face consequences, and yet has been inexplicably reticent to enforce these very agreements,” the report reads.

Accordingly, Godoy suggested adding explicit enforcement mechanisms to the Keep Washington Working Act, including a private right of action so that those harmed by the data sharing could receive restitution and potentially obtain court injunctions ordering a halt to illegal data access.

“We need to demand that Washington take action to at least protect us in the ways that it can,” Godoy said. “There's no way for Washington to just expel ICE agents from the state. That's not going to happen. But they don't need to serve us up to them on a silver platter with all of our data to make it so easy for them, to allow them to legitimate their arrests and their campaign of fear. So I think for electeds, this is your moment.”
Godoy also praised community members who have chosen to be involved in rapid response in defense of their immigrant neighbors.

articles.title: Seattle Social Housing Developer Advances First Construction Project
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: A new 20-unit apartment building in the Central District is set to make history as the first new development constructed by Seattle's three-year-old Social Housing Developer (SSHD). With a unanimous vote of the SSHD board to acquire a 7,800-square-foot property on E Yesler Way Thursday night, the vision of growing Seattle's housing stock with a new type of permanently affordable homes takes another major step forward.

The parcel set to be transformed into social housing, located at 2402 E Yesler Way, comes with an extra layer of meaning for Seattle housing advocates. It currently belongs to the family of former House Speaker Frank Chopp, who passed away in 2025 after a long career advocating around housing issues in the state legislature. Chopp's widow, Nancy Long, currently controls the property.

"It's very emotional because Frank was the first lawmaker that came out and supported social housing when House Our Neighbors ran the first initiative and [he] talked to multiple people on our behalf," SSHD Interim CEO Tiffani McCoy told The Urbanist following the vote. "So this is an incredible moment. I know that he would be proud, and it was really amazing that Nancy brought the property to us because she wanted it to be either affordable or social housing."
Construction is planned to start in 2027, with the building opening to tenants in 2028. The sale price for the land was $1.2 million, McCoy said, with a total project cost of $15 million.

This new project will be the SSHD's second housing project overall, ahead of what is expected to be an accelerated pace of property acquisition. Earlier this year, the developer took over operations of the 150-unit Elara at the Market along Western Avenue after purchasing that 2018 building for $60.9 million. More than 10,000 people applied for a chance to live in the first phase of rental units that were opened up to new applications this past spring.

Dedicated funding for the SSHD comes from a 5% payroll tax on annual compensation over $1 million, approved by Seattle voters in February 2025 with the passage of Proposition 1A. Annual revenues that were projected at approximately $50 million have proven extremely conservative, with $115 million coming in during the first year of collections. Those additional resources are set to allow the developer to scale up faster than previously anticipated.

McCoy, who previously served as the Co-Executive Director with House Our Neighbors, took over as Interim CEO in January after Roberto Jimenez, the first pick to lead the SSHD, was fired by the board . A key hire after Jimenez's departure was Ginger Segel, brought on as chief real estate development officer.

Central District House, as the developer is calling the E Yesler Way project, will be built to passive house standards, McCoy said. Architect and Baugruppen evangelist Michael Eliason, a past contributor to The Urbanist , remains the developer's director of design & policy.

Though details around planned design are scant right now, we do know that there are plans to approach the site a little differently than a normal market rate developer would. Thanks to a state law passed earlier this year – House Bill 1687 – social housing developers have expanded authority to request variances from existing zoning standards, authority that had previously only applied to public housing authorities.

"We are looking to utilize our new power under the Housing Cooperation Law to try to to try to move a setback so that we can be better neighbors and not have windows going directly next to the next door neighbor," McCoy said.
McCoy brought up the fact that the social housing developer's first project will be built in a neighborhood that has seen significant upheaval in its population over the past few decades.

"We also recognize the deep tension – it's in the Central District, it has a very racist past in there, and there's still massive displacement that is happening," McCoy said. "So we are excited about using a community preference plan, a really robust affirmative marketing plan, learning from folks that have done that so successfully there."

Central District House is just the start of planned property acquisitions by the Social Housing Developer, with plans advancing for work on both new build projects and acquisitions. A project pipeline that received a board vote Thursday, contingent on the issuance of bonds that will allow the payroll tax funding currently coming in to be leveraged much further, would see six new construction projects and four acquisitions move forward through the end of 2027.

"There's so much more we're doing that isn't public yet because we have to wait for our board of directors to let us talk about them," McCoy said. "I see a lot of momentum. There will be another announcement [of] between 50 and 250 units that is going to be coming in the end of the year, beginning of next year, and much more to come."

articles.title: Seattle Social Housing Developer Announces First Construction Project
articles.author: Guy Oron
paras: At a chilly morning press conference today, Seattle Social Housing Developer (SSHD) Interim CEO Tiffani McCoy announced plans for the agency’s first original construction project, a five-story apartment building in the Central District on the lot that used to belong to the late housing advocate Rep. Frank Chopp. Scheduled to open in 2028, the development will provide 20 units of housing, leased at a mix of affordable and market rate rents.

The Central District site is SSHD’s second official housing project, following the May acquisition of the 150-unit Elara at the Market in Belltown. The two are part of a rapidly expanding housing portfolio—the agency hopes to reach 1,000 units owned or in the pipeline by the end of 2027. McCoy says the SSHD has a third yet-to-be-announced acquisition that will bring the total to 300 units by the end of this year.

The announcement comes in the midst of SSHD’s herculean expansion effort—it’s looking to nearly triple its staffing over the next 14 months. All this is funded by a surprisingly large windfall from Seattle’s social housing tax on big corporations. But to keep the momentum, the agency needs to maintain its careful balancing act to keep our fickle local politicians on its side.

Established by two ballot initiatives, SSHD operates on a model that is relatively unique for public housing in the US. Instead of only serving poor households, residents from a broad range of class backgrounds are allowed to live in social housing, with wealthier tenants subsidizing the rents of their lower income neighbors.

As part of its mission SSHD is trying to be better than your average for-profit (or even non-profit) landlord. With the Elara, SSHD provided free ORCA transit cards to all residents, froze the rent for two years, and is working to end previous landlord Greystar’s practice of distributed utility building , which divides costs equally among tenants instead of based on usage. It has also hired a restorative justice manager to address intra-tenant conflicts.

SSHD spokesperson Lilly Ana Fowler says the efforts are already yielding results, with the building’s monthly turnover rate plummeting to below 2 percent, well below the average for market rate apartments. According to Fowler, 16 new low-income renters have moved into the Elara, and the agency plans for a total of 60 units in the building to be dedicated to households making less than 50 percent of the area median income.

The agency also wants to be a top-notch developer, pledging to use union labor for its constructions and follow green passive house and universal design standards. But these efforts don’t come cheap—at a total budgeted cost of $15 million, the new Central District apartments will cost roughly $750,000 a unit.

Part of this cost is also due to the mixture of units: The majority of homes in the building will be geared toward families, with 2 or 3 bedrooms. (Less than a third of all Seattle area rentals have two or more bedrooms, according to Zillow listing data ).

But, unlike most government agencies, SSHD is working with what could be considered a bounty of resources. Its primary source of revenue—the voter-approved 5 percent corporate surcharge on salaries above $1 million—delivered $136 million in tax revenue last year and an additional $59 million in the first half of 2026. This is about two and a half times more than was expected, and has put the agency under pressure to deliver.

Earlier this year, SSHD increased its 2027 year-end production goal by 70 percent. It currently has at least six additional new projects planned for the next year. In addition to the social housing tax money and rental income, the developer plans to issue a $270 million bond to pay for the portfolio expansion.

The SSHD will have to carefully navigate the choppy waters that are Seattle politics and rebuff politicians’ innate tendency to appropriate money for their own goals. To this end, the JumpStart payroll tax serves as a cautionary parable; Once upon a time most of its revenues was supposed to go to affordable housing, but now it’s mainly used to fill the budget deficit. Seattle City Council members are already circling the SSHD’s pot of money. At a September 29 budget committee meeting, Councilmember Bob Kettle floated the idea of diverting social housing tax money for other affordable housing projects. He can’t actually do that. Not yet, at least. The two-year period in which council members are not allowed to amend the tax expires in February 2027.

Several notable political allies stood with the SSHD at the press conference, including state legislators, Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck and a staff member from Councilmember Dionne Foster’s office. Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson did not send a representative, but she has previously shown strong support for the developer.
One notable absence was Council President Joy Hollingsworth, who represents the Central District and is rumored to be considering a mayoral run when Wilson’s term is up.

That hesitance may foreshadow a lukewarm reception to the neighborhood. The dynamics of development in the Central District are complicated and painful, with urban renewal policies displacing the majority of residents from the historic heart of Seattle’s Black community over the last 30 years. This adds a layer to the typical “NIMBY” concerns of having a new five-story building show up down the block.

At the press conference, Reverend Dr. Robert L. Jeffrey, Sr. of New Hope Missionary Baptist Church spoke supportively of the project, saying that SSHD’s community preference policy will give people with ties to the Central District “an opportunity to return home.”
“This type of initiative is what the Central District and the greater Seattle city needs,” Jeffrey said.
McCoy has indicated that SSHD will not shy away from pursuing taller developments in the future to maximize economies of scale and increase the number of people who can live in social housing.

One of the main pathways for SSHD to achieve this is by entering into housing cooperation agreements with the City, which allow it to bypass virtually all zoning requirements with a vote from the council. So to realize its ambitious goals, the SSHD will need to continue to thread the political needle.

The 7,800-square-foot Central District lot slated for development is a special case. It’s the home of former Washington State House Speaker Frank Chopp. During his time in the legislature, Chopp—who passed away last year—was a strong advocate for affordable housing. He also secured $200,000 in seed funding for the SSHD.

Chopp’s widow Nancy Long told The Stranger that due to high taxes, it didn’t make financial sense for her family to keep the property, but selling to a for-profit developer was off the table. The SSHD made a good prospective buyer, with its quick two-year development cycle, and cemented another brick in Chopp’s legacy.
“He would be very proud, I think, for this to be used for affordable housing,” Long says.
McCoy says the SSHD is talking with the City about relocating Chopp’s old blue heron-shaped tiny home and preserving it as a landmark.

Correction: An earlier version of this story stated that the agency plans for 60 units in the Elara to be dedicated to households making less that 80 percent median income. The units are for those making less than 50 percent of the area median income. We regret the error.

articles.title: The Stranger’s Noise Complaint: 4UST Collective
articles.author: Stranger Staff
paras: Welcome to Noise Complaint, The Stranger ‘s new audio and video music podcast featuring live performances right here at The Stranger HQ. Streamed live and released every other Friday, we invite a great band, musician, or wonderfully weird act to perform. Tune in, discover something new, and support art in your city.
Is 4UST Collective Seattle’s Next Big Hip-Hop Export?

Hip-hop typically hits harder when rappers are backed by actual ace musicians, as performances by the Roots and Shabazz Palaces (among others) prove. Seattle’s fast-rising 4UST (pronounced “forest”) uphold that claim with a grip of riveting live sets and recordings such as TR4IL MIX and All About the Growf . Led by MCs Webb Wavvy, D. Mikey, and Tyler Soze, they’re a tight crew in which all of the many moving parts smoothly click into place with a satisfying inevitability: intricate vocal arrangements, strong, fluid flows, clever wordplay, and instrumentation that expresses gritty funkiness, gripping suspense, or chill bluntedness from producer Qreepz, drummer/vocalist Mr. Hendrixxx, guitarist Aaron Lusher, bassist Palmer McDaniel, and others. Sure, 4UST have plenty of songs about weed, but the lyrics are cleverer than most about its importance to the (agri)culture—e.g., “All I need is some indica and I’m in da cut” from “Potluck.” With every track and gig, 4UST refute the common belief that pot induces laziness. articles.title: Despite Pushback, Updated RapidRide R Plans Include Scant Changes
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Updated plans for the future RapidRide R bus line between Downtown Seattle and Rainier Beach released this week include only a few changes to previous iterations of the project, with significant stop consolidation still planned along much of the eight-mile route despite community concerns.

The next RapidRide line to enter planning in Seattle, the R Line is set to replace the Route 7 along Rainier Avenue S by 2032, bringing upgrades to the Metro's second busiest bus line. Compared to an initial proposal put forward this summer , two stop pairs have been added for both northbound and southbound riders, including retained stops at Rainier Avenue S and S Walker Street and a new set of stops at Rainier Avenue S and S Grand Street. That change will help riders between Sound Transit's light rail stations at Judkins Park and Mount Baker more easily access bus stops, but riders further north or south could see longer walks to catch a frequent bus that is currently within easy reach.

If this plan is approved by the King County Council next month, the R Line will move forward with some major stops currently used by Route 7 riders not on the list, including 12th Ave S and Boren Ave S, Rainier Ave S and S Charles Street, and Rainier Ave S and S Andover Street. But the two stops between Judkins Park and Mount Baker do represent a response to community concerns about losing transit access along that specific stretch.

"The alignment proposal adds station pairs at Rainier Ave S & S Grand St and at Rainier Ave S & S Bayview St in response to updated ridership, new housing, community destinations, and public feedback, and retains the station pair at Rainier Ave S & S Walker St to serve nearby schools, the Lighthouse for the Blind, and riders affected by steep grades and difficult crossings," Metro's updated engagement summary notes. "Additionally, as design progresses, exact station locations will be determined by multiple conditions, including ongoing analysis and engagement."

The R Line has emerged as a major priority for King County Executive Girmay Zahilay, a bus line that connects neighborhoods across the council district he represented from 2020 to 2024. Before Zahilay took office, the R Line's budget was slashed by 25% in response to budget pressures at Metro, with a new total budget of $91.2 million.

Unlike most recent RapidRide lines including the under-construction I and J and Lines, King County does not plan to pursue federal matching funds , a fact that speaks to the current transit funding environment in D.C. But not being tethered to a USDOT grant agreement could potentially allow the County to move more quickly toward construction or implement upgrades in stages.

In releasing his biggest budget update since taking office last month, Zahilay proposed to advance $64.4 million in RapidRide R funding to the current two-year budget, in a move his office framed as intended to "build a strong partnership" with the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT), also planning roadway improvements along Rainier Avenue S that are set to be implemented in the early 2030s.

""Our South Seattle communities deserve fast, reliable transit service. Residents have been waiting over a decade for the RapidRide R Line, and we are moving with urgency to deliver on this generational investment that will greatly enhance mobility while also making critical safety upgrades,” Zahilay said in an announcement of the updated plan Thursday. “During Metro’s community engagement over the summer, we heard directly from seniors, people with disabilities, and families who were concerned about losing stops along Route 7. In response to that feedback, the alignment plan proposes two additional stops. We know this will be a change for neighbors who have relied on Route 7 for years, and we will continue listening to community and working to ensure the R line meets the diverse needs of residents and riders in the Southend.”

With fewer stops to make, the R Line will move more quickly along its route, on top of planned transit speed and reliability investments including transit signal priority (TSP) and additional bus-only lanes on top of the stretches already in place. But expected time savings data for a trip on the future R Line still has not been released by Metro, a key ask of transit advocates trying to weigh the trade-offs that come with stop consolidation.

Long stretches of bus lanes that had been envisioned when the R Line entered planning nearly a decade ago are now fully implemented , including a long stretch of northbound Rainier Avenue between S Edmunds Street in Columbia City and S Grand Street just south of I-90. But Metro and SDOT have not announced any plans for transit priority along S Jackson Street, one of the current Route 7's biggest pain points.

"The Rainier Valley stop consolidation decision-making was done with data that is now fairly out of date," a September 15 letter from the advocacy group Rainier Valley Safe Streets stated. "New studies that take into account current and future ridership enabled by the large apartment complexes that have been completed since the previous studies should be done. We recognize that stop consolidation is a difficult thing to get right, but densification of the Rainier Valley, especially near Judkins Park might justify decreased stop spacing."

Metro leaders – and County Councilmembers – are likely to face a push to consider restoring even more stop pairs along the corridor, given gaps of up to a half-mile that would be created. Even in an official letter of support included in the proposal transmitted to the King County Council, Seattle's Transit Riders Union (TRU) voiced concerns that the two new stop pairs weren't enough to mitigate impacts.

"We appreciate that Metro took community feedback into account and added back additional stops between Judkins Station and Mt Baker," the letter from TRU's bus and transit subcommittee noted. "We are still concerned by the large gaps created by consolidation which effectively choose to convert this route from its current attempt to be both a local and long distance service into an express bus skipping past parts of the south end. We would like to see this project go to further planning with wiggle room on which stops to move and remove."

It also remains to be seen how Metro will address riders south of S Henderson Street in Rainier Beach, along the so-called "Prentice Loop" only served by select Route 7 trips now. That area is currently served by Metro Flex microtransit service, an option that fills in the gaps in Metro's network but is absolutely not a replacement for fixed-route transit.

"Community members emphasized that the Prentice Loop and related neighborhood connections in the Rainier View and lower Rainier neighborhoods are essential for reaching schools, grocery stores, clinics, youth programs, religious centers, parks, and everyday destinations not located directly on Rainier Avenue S," the engagement summary stated. "Riders shared that existing local service helps seniors, riders with disabilities, youth, caregivers, and families access places that would otherwise require long and steep walks."
Thursday's announcement included some additional details about the future of transit service throughout broader Rainier Beach.

"Metro is also evaluating how to maintain strong and convenient transit connections for people traveling to and from areas south of South Henderson Street that will not be directly served by RapidRide R Line," the statement read, referencing potential changes to the Route 106, 107, and the 9. "Before the RapidRide R Line launches, Metro will engage communities south of South Henderson Street to better understand local travel needs, priorities, and important destinations and connections."

Even though a vote to sign off on the planned stop locations is planned for next month, the County Council will not actually be required to sign off on any adjustments to the R Line's stops, with the proposed ordinance only set to require notification.

"Before the implementation of RapidRide R Line service, the executive shall notify the King County council and the city of Seattle of any substantial changes to station locations," the draft ordinance states. "Following the implementation of RapidRide R Line service, the Metro transit department shall consult with the city of Seattle before making any changes to the routing or station locations."
After that vote, the R Line will advance into the next stage of planning, where Metro will align route upgrades with the project's reduced budget.

"Specific scope changes haven’t been finalized yet," Metro spokesperson Al Sanders told The Urbanist last month . "Those decisions will come in the next phase of design, after we confirm the route and stop locations. Once that foundation is set, we’ll be able to evaluate which capital improvements provide the greatest benefit within the appropriated budget and make informed decisions about what to carry forward into design."

articles.title: Friday Roundtable: Fall Foliage
articles.author: Michael Smith
paras: The leaves are finally starting to fall and there is no better place to admire King County’s incredible scenery than from a historic Metro bus. The annual Metro Employees Historic Vehicle Association (MEHVA) Fall Foliage Tour is back this year on October 25. Ride on one of the historic buses in MEHVA’s fleet through the Cascade foothills. Buses depart from 6th Ave S & S Royal Brougham Way (one block from Stadium station) at 11am and will return around 3pm. Tickets cost $10 and the group will stop for lunch along the way.

If you prefer to stay in Seattle, the Washington Park Arboretum is incredible this time of year. The arboretum is located just west of Madison Park, near stops for routes 8, 11, 43, 48, and the G Line. UW station is the closest Link station, about a 20 minute walk from the park.

articles.title: The Best Restaurants in Seattle’s University District
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: The University District is frequently (and wrongly) written off as a place only college kids would want to eat; the story usually goes that it’s rife with sketchy lunch counters, nondescript multinational fast food chains, and an overabundance of boba tea joints. But the truth is that the U District is one of the city’s essential dining destinations, with a dizzying array of global cuisines concentrated on its main street, University Way (confusingly known as the Ave).

There’s Korean food, regional Chinese specialties, Indian groceries, Vietnamese kitchens, falafel windows, and more on nearly every block. And practically everything is both affordable and genuinely good, so figuring out where to eat in this neighborhood is more a matter of grappling with the paradox of choice than anything else. So, here’s a short list to get you started.

articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.

articles.title: The 38 Best Restaurants in Seattle
articles.author: <name>Sophie Grossman</name>
paras: “Where should I eat in Seattle?” Whether you’re a first-time visitor or a lifer, that question is seemingly simple but the answers are infinitely complex. Some of the main factors to consider are the type of food, price point, neighborhood, and occasion. That’s why Eater’s map of the 38 best restaurants in Seattle exists. This curated list of suggestions attempts to capture the diversity of the food scene in the Seattle metro area, from English pubs serving cumin-y lamb neck meat pies to Indian street food takeout spots, from classic French bistros to modern sushi bars, and so much more. Every place on the list has been open for at least six months, proving its merit.

Like many menus, this map updates every quarter — removal from the Eater 38 doesn’t mean a restaurant isn’t still awesome and won’t return in the future. New to the map as of August 2026: unassuming neighborhood gem Three Sacks Full; seafood-focused French bistro L’Oursin; and La Cabaña, where you can find some of the city’s best pupusas.

articles.title: The Best Restaurants in Ballard
articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: Once a quiet working-class Nordic-American neighborhood, Ballard is now a nightlife, shopping, and restaurant destination. Boutiques and cocktail bars line Ballard Avenue (home to one of Seattle’s few year-round farmers markets ), and townhomes and high-rises have taken the place of single-family homes. Some of the best restaurants and bars in the city can be found here, along with almost (almost!) too many breweries , which is why if you walk far enough inland you can literally smell the hops. Where else in Seattle can you find Detroit-style pizza, Sri Lankan cocktails, and a congee specialist?
